facts.fact: Heroine is Neela, 27, odiyan of the Resin House, ledger number Seventeen. She does not know her birth name.
Love interest is Devan, 32, warden of Kettamala hill fort and the queen's border commander for the Monkey Pass.
Neela's night-shape is a leopard. Ammu's is a jackal, Vellan's a sloth bear, Kirri's a civet. Shapes are fixed at the first turning and never chosen.
An odiyan turns only after sunset, by smearing nightbark resin on throat and wrists. She turns back at first light and cannot turn back early, turn by day, or speak while in shape.
A witness is anyone who has seen a turning (dusk or dawn) with their own eyes. Seeing only the animal does not make someone a witness.
A witness who speaks the night-shape aloud in the odiyan's hearing, while she is in shape and before dawn, cages her for life. Intent does not matter. Non-witnesses cannot cage.
Caged odiyans stay animals for life and their human minds fade over about a year. No caging is ever undone.

Self-naming: during a dusk turning, an odiyan speaks her own night-shape to one chosen person looking at her. It voids all other witnesses, a caging then needs both their voices, her ledger witness entry burns, and she is marked rogue. It can be done only once in a life.
A self-named pair feel each other's wounds for life. A cut opens as a welt on the other, and a mortal wound drags the other toward death.
A ledger page in a true witness's resin-ink gives its holder a witness's power when read aloud at night in the odiyan's hearing. Pages cannot be forged.
Handing a page to its own subject requires the holder to read it aloud in full by daylight before her. A page held by its own subject cannot be used against her.
Each ledger page has the odiyan's intake roll (birth name, birth village) fastened to it. Self-naming burns only the witness entry. Burning the whole page destroys the intake roll.
Going a full moon without resin brings the ache: fever, night-sweats and split nails. Never fatal. Resin can be forced on an unwilling odiyan, which tears the resin scars.
Every odiyan has pale ridged resin scars at the throat and inner wrists.
Marma and kalari are skill, not magic. A marma strike can kill in human form.
Kettamala is a laterite hill fort above the Monkey Pass. Its west stair has a parrot newel post with a broken beak. The cistern chain clanks on the hour.
The warden's chamber has west-facing teak shutters, and the third slat creaks. The fort kalari is a sunken earthen pit below the east wall.
The Resin House is in the Blackbark Wood, a day's hard ride from Kettamala, and has kennels for caged odiyans.
Kodiyur is the royal port capital of Varanad. The palace sits on a sea cliff and the harbour tower fires a noon gun.
The monsoon closes the Monkey Pass and the hill roads for about four months.
Neela was married to Devan as the ward of the Chirayil pepper house, at a match pressed by the queen's council and proposed by Councillor Ittan.
Ammu, 25, is Neela's guild-sister, raised beside her since age 5, and calls her chechi. Ammu witnessed Neela's first turning.
Asha, Devan's younger sister and second at the fort, was killed at 22 on the west stair six years before book 1.
Janu, 61, steward of Kettamala, raised Devan and Asha after their mother died.
Captain Muthu, 35, is Devan's second-in-command and secretly writes monthly reports to the queen's household.
Ruler is Queen Nirmala of Varanad, 54. The guild master is Chathu, 61, not an odiyan. Councillor Ittan, 49, is Keeper of the Passes.
Neela wears a plain gold wedding bangle from the wedding onward.
Forged pass-tokens reaching Thurai raiders bear genuine council wax. The queen seals in green wax.
Kirri wears a silver anklet, which she still wears when caged in the kennels.
Neela's contract is her twelfth. Twelve completed contracts are promised to earn release.
Book 1 opens on the wedding day, about 40 days before the monsoon closes the pass, which is Neela's contract deadline.
Devan has not sparred a living person in eight years. He drills kalari alone every dawn.
Border wardens are taught the odiyan witness rule. Devan knows it from the start.
The coastal raiders come from Thurai, a rival kingdom ruled by sea lords.
The Resin House owns the only nightbark groves and rations resin. Rogues must steal resin or buy it cut with lamp oil.
Kannan is a goat-boy of about nine or ten; Chinna runs the kitchen door; Raiu is a young guard who holds the corridor torch outside the warden's chamber.
Devan tells Neela the night guard layout: two on the west stair, four at the padippura, six on the wall in pairs, changing on the third clank after the middle watch.
Devan lays his sword on the floor on Neela's side of the bed, hilt toward her; the grip is plain wire, worn at the thumb.
Neela carries the guild's leopard tooth sewn into her waistband and the resin in a corked flask in a fold of her cloth.
Devan says he took four months and asked twice to learn Raiu's name.
Devan first smelled nightbark resin at twenty, from a sealed jar passed around a classroom during his border training on the witness rule.
Janu says it is the first time in eleven years Devan has asked for food himself.
Gopan is the old keeper of the cistern chain and wheel, nineteen years in the post, who missed one hour in 'the fever year'.
Bhaskaran is the sergeant at the padippura. Unni is a thin young guard whose mother sells salt fish in the lower village.
The day watch changes on the sixth clank of the cistern chain after dawn.
Pepper is Kannan's white goat, who bites.
Janu says Devan used to have a kalari partner and now trains alone, a gap of eight years.
The hounds of Kettamala number fourteen and sleep in a long kennel behind the stables; before the wedding they ran the yard loose from dusk to dawn.

Bhaskaran passed a salt-and-cloth cart from the coast through his gate at the last new moon on the strength of a council-wax tally, and the tally number matches the one found in the dead raider's satchel.
Genuine council wax is dull brick red, pressed with a pepper-sprig mark, and poured with clove oil so it does not crack in damp. The forged tally's wax is about a month old.
Devan tells Neela the pass-seller is someone on the queen's council and that he does not know who; he says the raiders' next targets are the coast-side villages.
Neela finds a gap of about thirty counts under the far wall when the lower wall pair swings inward, and one sentry paces the walk above the warden's window.
Bhaskaran led the patrol to the second ford at dawn after a herdsman reported men there.

Neela notices that Devan's only untrue statement is 'Rain' at dusk under a clear sky; it is the single thing he will not say plainly. She links it to the kennelled hounds as both being about the dark.

Neela notices that 'Rain' at dusk under a clear sky is the one answer Devan gives that is not an answer; it sounds like a forecast but fits nothing in the sky. She links it and the kennelled hounds as both being about the dark. She does not conclude he lies.
Kannan's loft sits over the kennel wall; the hounds howl until the middle watch.
Chinna sleeps on a mat at the kitchen door; the granary has a farm lock.
Janu says Devan has slept badly for eight years.
On the night of chapter 4 Neela counts thirty-seven nights left before the pass closes.
Captain Muthu was Devan's kalari partner before Devan stopped sparring eight years ago, and he asks for a round every seventh day.
Kannan's mother is named Bindu and sings; Neela learned this from women at the well.
Neela's cover guardian is Kunjan Chirayil, who kept the Chirayil north warehouse in Kodiyur.
Asha came to the fort at nineteen and in her first month wrote every recruit's name and mother's village on a slate.

The sentry Devan has pulled off the rampart is the one above the warden's window (ch 4 placement), not below it as the outline says; Devan lifts the shutter bar and leaves it against the wall that night.

Devan has the sentry above the warden's window (ch 4 placement, not below as the outline says) pulled, but leaves the shutter bar in its usual place across the shutters; Neela must lift it herself as on previous nights.
Janu found Asha's body on the west stair the morning after she was killed.
Devan spent two years at a border school, where he learned the witness rule and first smelled nightbark resin.
Devan's father is dead; Devan respected him, and fondness came after his death.
Neela wears a day kasavu from her trousseau on the terraces and tears its gold border to bind Kannan's hand.
Queen Nirmala's green wax seal is pressed with a small sunbird, wings spread. The wax smells of crushed leaf, not clove.

The palace gift is a silver betel set in a sandalwood box: tray, lidded lime box and an areca cutter with a sunbird handle. Devan has it locked in the granary and keeps the cut wax seal in his sleeve.
Sudhi is the palace rider who brought the sandalwood box. Maniyamma and Thankappan carried the chests. The Chirayil gift is a five-cup brass standing lamp with a bird on the stem.

The guild meeting stone is a knee-high split laterite slab with a lightning scar and a cup cut in its top, in the pala grove at the top of the second spur above the terraces. A jackal scent-mark is fresh on it.
The guild's jackal-call signal: three short yips, a pause, one long rising note means 'tomorrow, I will find you'. Neela and Ammu practised it as children.
Neela concludes the household's weak hour is the last dark hour before the day watch, when lanterns burn low and Raiu nods at the corridor torch, but that Devan wakes and rises for the kalari in it.
Neela counts thirty-five nights left on the night of chapter 6.
Neela turns back at first light crouched on the warden's window ledge, and the ginger tom cat with a notched ear walks the parapet above it where the sentry used to stand.

Neela believes the household's weak hour is the last dark hour before first light, when the night wall pairs have stood longest, lanterns burn low and Raiu nods at the corridor torch. She knows Devan's early rising only from Janu and the pit lamps, never having seen it, since she is always out on the hill then. At first light she hears him abed again and is unsure. This corrects and replaces F075 (the day watch changes six clanks after dawn, F045).
The rampart above the warden's window has been empty two nights by the night of chapter 6, since Devan pulled the sentry in chapter 5. Neela notes it but no longer calls it luck.
Before each of her eleven completed contracts, Master Chathu sent Neela a tin of warm jaggery-sesame sweets 'for luck'. She learned around the fifth that a gift is the start of a bill.
Every guild meeting stone is cut with a cup in its top; marks are left in it or things under it.
Neela and Ammu practised the jackal call as children, at eleven and nine, in the yard behind the sheds, until Chathu told them the Resin House had no use for dogs.
Devan's sleeping breath has a small hitch a third of the way through each long count. On the dawn of chapter 6 it hitched on the exact beat of Neela's laugh; she files it as chance.
Ammu's market cover is 'Valli', a coast-side pepper trader's girl who came up with the last cart before the passes close.

Parukutty is a soldier's widow in the lower village with a six-year-old daughter and a nine-year-old son; her husband Raman, a spearman, died on Devan's patrol in spring. She owes the salt factor six and a half measures plus a tally fee.
Muthu goes down to the lower market with the garrison's purse on market days, and tells Neela that Devan hates market day.
Chathu's message to Neela: the writ is on the road; after it lands every day counts double; if the account is open when the pass closes he will force resin on her and read her page aloud at dusk.
Neela counts thirty-four nights left on the morning of chapter 7.
The tune Ammu hums is a fishing song with the refrain 'Pull and pull, the tide is coming in'.
Raiu is nineteen, with an unruly cowlick. From this chapter Devan posts him at the head of the stair after dusk, and the corridor lamp outside the warden's chamber is left unlit.

The council keeps seven tally seals, each cut with a private mark at the sprig's stem: four have a bar, three have a dot with a split under it. The forged tally bears the dot-and-split, so it came from one of three boxes or a copy. Devan lifted beeswax impressions to compare.

By custom the pass-seal passes to the fort's captain when a warden dies, but an old charter line gives it to a wife in trust if the warden has one. The returned marriage writ states this plainly: she holds it until the council names a new warden. No warden has married in office in living memory.
The marriage writ returns from Kodiyur by a registry courier in registry blue, who will not climb to the keep and gives the case to Unni at the gate.

A goat path leaves the cart road left of a lightning-split boulder at the Monkey Pass gorge below the last pass village, climbs the scree and the shoulder, and drops through thorn past an old well to the lower waystation. Neela knows it without a map and cannot say how.
The lower waystation is a low laterite house with a well, a carters' shed and a trodden yard; it stands empty between seasons.

Six men rested at the waystation two nights ago and left north before dawn on foot; Neela reads their boots as a trained soldier's heel, a rider's wear and new coast-stitched soles, so they were fed and brought most of the way rather than walking from the sea.
Kesu is a one-eyed grandfather in one of the pass villages.
Neela counts thirty-two nights left on the morning of chapter 9, the day after the writ arrives.
The west stair has forty-four steps from the lower court to the landing below the passage; the eleventh step rings hollow over a drain slot, and the rail is pala wood.
The parrot newel stands at the foot of the west stair, a forearm long, its broken beak worn smooth as a river stone.
Janu keeps ten paces from the foot of the west stair and does not seem to know she does it.
Before the wedding the warden's shutters stood open every night it did not storm, by his father's rule that a room should breathe; they were not barred even the winter his mother died.
Chinna has a wager running on why the warden bars his shutters. The fort's theories are privacy, damp-madness and Janu's old tale.
Neela counts thirty-one nights left on the night of chapter 10, and decides to skip resin the following night.
The kindi on Neela's side of the bed is found full each night with its spout toward the pillow; she assumes Janu's girls fill it.

Lantana grows in thick banks down the slope of the east path to the fort kalari; Gopan keeps meaning to cut it. The pit is about twenty paces across and shoulder-deep, shored with laterite blocks, with lamps in niches round the rim and steps cut in the north side.
Neela tells Devan she learned to read feet from 'a man who guarded pepper', one of two guards at Kunjan Chirayil's warehouse (cover story). Devan accepts it.
Muthu asks Devan for a round every seventh day and Devan refuses every time; Devan states he has not sparred for 'eight years in the spring'.

Asha's room is the last door at the end of the south passage, shut six years; Janu holds the key on a cord and could not enter it herself. Contents: a camphor-wood chest with a green brass hasp, a cot, a stool, and a leather cap on a peg.
Asha's slate, with recruits' names and mothers' villages in faded chalk (matches F063), lies on top of the chest; the name Unni is on it, and Unni now holds the gate.

Asha's notes (forty or fifty, tied in red thread) are each signed with a drawn parrot of five strokes with a whole beak; she drew the west-stair newel 'mended' because she thought a broken beak insulted the bird.

Asha's first forged token is a split-ash tally stick wrapped in oilcloth with the red thread, bearing council wax with the dot-and-split mark matching Devan's beeswax impression of Bhaskaran's tally (F091). A note with it says: 'First one. Not yet. Need a second to be sure. Tell nobody at the gate.'
Devan did not know Asha had kept the first token; he had assumed it was taken by whoever killed her.
Asha was four years younger than Devan; Neela laughs at her note about Thursday sparring, where she 'took both points'.
Devan's last found note of Asha's reads: 'If you're reading this, I was right, and it's ugly. Say it anyway. The truth protects whoever finds it.' He withholds it from Neela.
The palace rider who takes the fort's post down is Sudhi (matches F072), who brings the royal post every ninth day.
Muthu hands Sudhi a letter sealed in plain grey wax with no mark, and says it is to his mother in Kodiyur; he pauses a half-breath before laughing. Devan believes him.
Eravi is the stooped fort physician who bleeds Devan twice and despairs.
Devan's raider arrow-graze is along the outside of his left forearm. The arrowhead was dung-smeared, so the wound festers with red lines up the arm.
A cotton curtain hangs inside the warden's chamber window, behind the shutters.
Neela counts twenty-nine nights left on the night of chapter 13. Janu opened the shutters that evening by Devan's father's rule that a sick room breathes.
Neela had intended to leave her guild report at the meeting stone for Ammu on the night of chapter 13, and missed it to stay with Devan.
Devan has been feeding the notched ginger tom off the table since the second week and has never mentioned it; Neela, as the other one, knows this.
In fever Devan says 'cat' repeatedly and once says the name Asha. Neela hears it in shape and takes it as raving.

Before tonight Devan has watched Neela turn ten times, always through his lashes with a sleeper's face. In ch13 the fever leaves his lids half open and she studies his face for one breath without reading him.

At first light after ch13 Ammu, in jackal shape on the second spur, gives the guild call (three yips, pause, one rising note: 'tomorrow, I will find you') after finding the stone empty. Neela does not stand.

In the last dark before first light after ch13, Ammu, in jackal shape on the second spur, gives the guild call (three yips, pause, one rising note: 'tomorrow, I will find you') after finding the stone empty. Neela hears it in shape and cannot answer. At dawn she reads 'tomorrow' as the coming day and expects Ammu at the gate by the gate-bell as Valli. This replaces the earlier first-light version.
When Janu returns and asks where Neela is, Devan tells her flatly that he sent Neela to sleep. Neela, behind the curtain in shape, hears the lie and takes it for fevered kindness.
Neela keeps a cache in a cleft of rock under the second spur: a day cloth, a shawl and a water gourd, hidden after she collapsed beside Devan's bed in ch13, so she can turn back away from the ledge.

The two raider scouts keep a cold camp (no fire) on the lip above the shelf in the lower narrows, with bows and a wrapped bronze signal mirror meant to flash the patrol's count to others beyond the cut. Who waits beyond is not known.

The scouts carry newly struck Varanad silver (sprig on one face, sharp milled edge, never handled) and a forged split-ash tally with real council wax that smells of clove. Devan notes the coins are unspent and takes the satchel and coin as evidence.
A scout's knife cuts a thin line across Neela's shoulder in leopard shape; it reopens as she turns back and she bleeds a little.
Valli (Ammu) did not come to the gate on the day after the fever broke, though Neela expected her ('tomorrow').
The 'pepper-store cat' is the fort's notched ginger tom, which Devan feeds. Janu says it has caught nothing since 'the fever year'.
Devan's patrol numbers eleven riders, and Raman's death in spring happened in single file under the shelf in the lower narrows.
Neela knows the lower narrows and the shelf only by sight from the east terraces and by hearsay of its going; she has not crossed it before this night.

Neela drops the satchel on the patrol path deliberately: Asha's note asked for a second token, so Devan gets it, and a bag on the path makes the camp read as raiders rather than a cat-kill. She knows it tells Devan someone stood there before him.
The first monsoon storm breaks about eight nights after ch14. Neela has twenty nights left and Devan says he has watched her for twenty days.

For eight nights since the narrows, Neela as the other one has worked the ridge beyond the cut looking for whoever waits there; on the storm night she tracks two couriers with a pack pony and loses them in the rain.
Neela keeps a plain six-inch guild knife in the gap between mattress and bed frame on her side.

Devan has stated he deduced her purpose (sent to kill him) from the council-pressed match and her habits, and swore the silence offer on Asha's name; he asked for the name of whoever bought his death and offered it once.

On the storm night Neela does not use her cache under the second spur: it lies a long climb the wrong way up the slope and the cleft would be running with rain, and she misjudges the hour, believing she has two hours of night when dawn is already near, so she runs for the ledge.

At the border school in his second year, an instructor read Devan's class a seized guild courier's letter whose kindly tone ('a kindness of your own to return') illustrated how masters leash members by mentioning a debt.
Devan once swore on the west stair, the day Asha died, never to be the one who holds a throat; Devan says nothing of this to Neela.
Neela counts nineteen nights left on the dusk of ch16 and expects the unfed ache to arrive in nine or ten days.
Biscuit is Sudhi's pony; Appu, nine, is the groom who loves it.
Devan has known since the second week that Neela keeps a knife under the mattress on her side, and has never moved it.

Devan tells Neela that the Keeper of the Passes' office holds one of the three dot-and-split seal boxes, without naming the three keepers; he lists the three seal boxes and Sudhi the palace rider as suspects.
Ittan has written Devan a kind letter every season for six years but has never climbed to Kettamala; the council normally sends a clerk to seal the pass.
Neela tells Devan she calls her night-self 'the other one', her first disclosure of the word to anyone.
Devan tells Neela to say the market-day cover for her absence: Parukutty's daughter has a cough (true).
Kirri's silver anklet had its bells cut off; she never took it off, even to bathe. She swore to send it in a fish-basket as a sign once she had her boat.
Ammu has written eleven times to Kirri's address and Chathu answers only 'Kirri is where she wished to be, child.'

Seven wells is a pebble-tossing game on a plank with seven hollows; a pebble counts only if it strikes the hollow's wall and then drops, and rivals' stones may be flicked out. Cheats get a ladle rap on the knuckles.
Devan played seven wells once at eight and Asha beat him, which he says was by cheating.
Neela counts sixteen nights left on the day of chapter 18, with the meeting at the stone by day and the game that evening.
Kannan gives Neela a white pebble from the game to keep.
As children Neela and Ammu saw Vellan's bear-shape stand over them in the Resin House yard, and they have seen other girls taken to the kennels as punishment. Neela already knows members are caged.
Chinna's kitchen-door gossip reached Ammu: the bride was seen at the window at dawn in her sleeping cloth.
Neela's nails begin to itch at the quick on day sixteen, a warning before the ache. Ammu has waited about three weeks at the inn.
Ammu carries a twist of paper with Chathu's message and keeps it; it is never handed to Neela.
A split reed laid across the cup of a guild meeting stone is Resin House shorthand for 'show me': the sender wants to watch the work done.

The east rampart has a low laterite cistern housing holding the chain and wheel, a low shoulder in the wall east of it, and a narrow east stair cut into the wall's thickness with a lamp niche at the second turn.
Devan arranged for the wall pair on the east stretch to be held at the padippura by a cart dispute, and says he noticed Neela's lips move as she counts steps and exits.
Neela tells Devan she counts his sleeping-breath hitch lately.

The cistern housing on the east rampart is a low laterite structure whose roof stands about chest-high to a man; Neela judges its lee hides the east-rampart spot from the grove, but the grove lies downslope and a watcher there sees over the roof.
Gopan's cistern chain jams in damp; Devan took the wheel apart as a genuine reason to be on the east rampart.
The stair to the hall has fourteen steps and Neela takes the turn on the eleventh, which Devan has noticed since the first week.
Neela leaves her day cloth and flask in the lamp niche at the second turn of the east stair before turning.
Ammu watches from the grove edge in jackal shape after dusk, having left the split reed at the stone at dawn in human form; her eyes stay fixed on the housing door where Neela and Devan kissed.

The cistern housing on the east rampart is man-high, with a door Devan steps out of. The pala grove and meeting stone stand on the second spur, higher than the rampart (consistent with F073). Neela judged the lee from the wall-walk, where the housing flank and the low parapet shoulder looked solid, but from the grove Ammu looks down onto the spot and nothing hides it. This replaces the earlier chest-high-roof, downslope-grove version.
Chathu's deadline: if the account is still open at the new moon, nine nights from the morning of chapter 20, he sends Vellan.
Ammu follows Neela's scent to the cache under the second spur at dawn and promises to write nothing to Chathu for one week; she will leave a reed in the cup on the seventh night.

Old tappers' song verse: 'Tap the bark when the sun goes low, / let the black sap run and the lantern burn slow. / What the dusk has taken, the dusk will say, / the name given back at the closing of day.' Neela has never heard the last verse.

Gopan taught Devan at sixteen to hold a river pebble in the cheek on long cistern watches so a sleeper cannot form clean words. From chapter 20 Devan keeps one in his cheek every night Neela smears resin, from dusk until she is back at first light.
Ammu believes Neela's lie that Devan does not know what she is.
Ammu's seventh-night signal is an unsplit reed left in the cup of the meeting stone, meaning she has kept her word (distinct from the split reed 'show me', F162).

Neela tells Ammu a second lie: Devan did not turn round on the rampart because he was facing the terraces and thinks the passing animal was the fort's notched ginger tom. Ammu accepts it because she wants to.

Devan answers the rampart kiss aloud: he stayed still because she ran, not because he did not want to follow; he will not ask at dusk with resin on her, and tells her to find him in daylight when she wants it.
A thatched tack room beside the fort kalari, with two roof leaks and two buckets, is where Devan restrings bows on the rain-locked day.

The raider captain Devan killed at 24 was taken at the lower ford after a village was burned; Muthu opened his arm and saw the killing. Devan struck the marma point in the notch below the ear with two fingers.
Devan has filled Neela's kindi himself every night since the second week, spout toward the pillow because she reaches left-handed.
Neela skips resin on the rain night of chapter 21 because the rain washed the scent from the hill, so Devan does not use the pebble that night. Her nails itch.
Neela tells Devan she was six when taken, lost her birth name on the road, and thinks Chathu has it in a ledger.
Asha counted stairs in the dark because she believed numbers kept the dark from filling in (she was terrified of the dark). Devan recalls this while Neela counts stairs in her sleep.
Raiu's mother is dead; Chinna has a bad hip.
Question-game rule: either player may say 'I won't answer' once in total, and the other lets it lie.
After midnight on the rain night Neela wakes, presses her itching nails and says aloud 'Eight nights to the new moon'. Devan hears it but does not know what ends then.

The wall-at-back sleeping habit dates from Asha's death (six years); his bad sleep dates from the ford (eight years). Neela listed only 'the kennels, and a big man's shadow in the yard' as childhood fears, without naming Vellan.
The guild keeps a watcher in the pass village who logs each night which shapes are abroad on the hill; a night with no shape out on an open contract reads as refusal and is reported to Chathu.
Chathu sends the carrier a balance sheet for every open contract; Ammu copied one entry from the carrier's satchel: 'Balance due from the Keeper on the widow's seal.'
Chapter 22 is the second consecutive night Neela skips resin (the rain night of ch 21 was the first) and seven nights remain to the new moon.
Devan has a puckered white seam at the ribs from the raider captain's knife at the ford, before the captain knelt.

The guild keeps a watcher in the pass village who logs scent-posts, not faces or shapes: each dawn he walks the hill edge and reads which of an odiyan's marks have gone fresh. A night with no fresh marks on an open contract reads as refusal and is reported to Chathu. Ammu covered the second skipped night by laying her own scent over Neela's posts; the rain night of ch 21 already stood logged as a gap.

Chathu sends the carrier a balance sheet for every open contract; Ammu tore a strip from the foot of the carrier's satchel copy, in Chathu's resin-ink hand: 'Balance due from the Keeper on the widow's seal.'
Chapter 22 is the second consecutive night Neela skips resin (the rain night of ch 21 was the first) and seven nights remain to the new moon.
Devan has a puckered white seam at the ribs from the raider captain's knife at the ford, before the captain knelt.

Nightly stone signal during Ammu's week of silence: the other one's scent-mark in the cup of the meeting stone means 'still working'; Ammu leaves her own mark to say she looked. Her unsplit reed (F177) is still due on the seventh night. Ammu turned back at first light and Neela reached her an hour later.
Devan has not lain with anyone since before the ford, eight years ago.
Chathu held Neela's wrist at her first resin. In the second week Devan asked about her scars and she lied 'a fall from a cart'; she tells him the truth in ch 22.
Ittan's name stood first on the council letter that proposed the match; Devan noted it at the time as a kind man's name.
Ittan's genial letter said he would come himself this season to seal the pass and see how the match has prospered; Devan read it aloud to Neela one night.
The pass closes in eight days from the morning of chapter 23 (the sealing day); the new moon falls before it.
Border charter custom: on sealing day every cart leaving through the padippura is searched before it goes, with no exception written for the Keeper.
Neela tells Devan the slip came from a guild-sister who tore it off a carrier's satchel, and says she will not say more; Devan does not ask.

From the morning of chapter 23 the new moon is six nights off (consistent with ch22's seven), the Keeper is due two days after it, and the pass is sealed in eight days; the rains close the road behind the sealing.
Border custom: on sealing day every cart through the padippura, in or out, is opened and searched; no exception is written for the Keeper (aligns F204).
Kodiyur is four days at a hard ride from Kettamala.
Neela refuses to name her source beyond 'a guild-sister' and does not name Ammu to Devan; she refers to 'my sister's page' on the next leaf of the ledger.
Devan sees Captain Muthu hand a grey-sealed letter to a lathered rider at the padippura off post day (the ninth-day post is Sudhi's); Muthu is quiet, not laughing.

Devan objects that the Keeper's office holds a dot-and-split seal box by right, so finding the box proves nothing. Neela answers that the proof is what Ittan carries with it: blank split-ash tallies already waxed with the dot-and-split, unregistered in any clerk's book, matching Asha's token and the scouts' satchel tally. This sets up Ittan's arrest with forged tokens in ch29.
Muthu's mother has been dead four years; Devan stood at her pyre. So Muthu's claim that his grey-wax letters are to his mother is a plain lie.
This chapter takes place the day after ch23 morning: five nights remain to the new moon.

Vellan is told by the guild watcher that Devan lays his sword hilt toward Neela, and he sat at the meeting stone in human form in daylight, having told Ammu he would keep the stone that day. Ammu stays at her inn as Valli.
Vellan's carved bird is plum-sized, pale wood, wing folded, head turned, beak whole, and smells of scorched tamarind (resin) from his hands.
Neela tells Devan Vellan's name, rough age, the new-moon deadline and the collar threat, but refuses to name his night-shape. Devan accepts without asking.

REPLACES the earlier F212. Muthu's mother is alive and writes to him once a month, on the ninth-day post. Devan knows Muthu goes quiet when he lies (since the kalari pit as boys), so two grey-wax letters in two days, the first on an off post day, make him suspect Muthu is Ittan's man. He decides to keep Muthu close and frames the sealing-day gate post as an honour: Muthu will open the Keeper's boxes himself.
Kettamala's garrison is about sixty soldiers.

Devan moves Raiu from the head of the stair to the warden's chamber door; he is to be at the stair after dusk with a second man, and Devan doubles the watch. The carved bird is found cold on Neela's pillow, so Vellan placed it by day while she was away, and Neela reasons he means four nights, not five.

Vellan says 'the watcher says' that Devan lays his sword hilt toward Neela. Neela registers that the watcher (F194) only reads scent-posts on the hill edge and cannot see inside a barred chamber, so someone inside Kettamala is feeding the guild. She tells Devan: 'Someone in your house talks to mine.' Retires stale F212 (Muthu's mother dead) and supersedes F214 and F219 on this point.

Single post: Devan puts Raiu on the warden's chamber door from the night of ch24, with two more men at the west stair head and extra pairs on the wall. The bird was placed on Neela's pillow by Vellan between the hour she went up the second spur and the hour she returned; the bird is found cold. Neela reasons he means four nights, not five.

Devan privately plans sealing day as a test of Muthu: he will stand beside the cart himself and set Bhaskaran to open the second box, watching whether Muthu's hands hesitate. Neela nearly says Vellan's night-shape ('He's a—') and stops; Devan's eyes go to the west stair newel. Garrison about sixty (replaces draft F218).
Devan did not see Vellan turn: the bend in the west stair hid the change, so Devan is not Vellan's witness and the word is only a word to him. He infers a bear from the claw marks.
Vellan's blade cuts Devan across the left ribs, with a blackbark-gall poison that spreads as a black thread from the wound. The physician Eravi gives it about three days.
Raiu dies on the west stair from four claw furrows across his chest. His death is permanent.
Neela skipped resin on the new-moon night to stay human and guard Devan, and three of her nails have split to the quick, so the ache has started.
Neela saddles a grey mare in the fort stable. She tells Muthu to bring Devan after her if she is not back by the second dusk.
The antidote is made by Chathu himself and kept in a locked cupboard in the tapping shed at the Resin House. Neela can open the lock.

Before dusk Devan sent Raiu down to the lower court for lamp oil because the west stair lamps had run dry, which is why Raiu reaches the stair from below at the first sound of steel. The two men at the stair head had orders to hold it whatever they heard and move only once the bear was gone.
Vellan tells Devan that his house keeps count of the eight years since he struck anyone, further evidence of the inside informant (F220).

Neela's ache has been building for weeks (F145, F160). The nails splitting on the morning of ch25 sharpened it; skipping resin on the new-moon night did not cause them. She tells Devan she trusts Muthu with his body, not his secrets, because she has no one else.
Pachan is a Resin House hunter who once gave ten-year-old Neela his sweet at the long table. Hunters carry hooked poles, nets and iron rings on chains.
Chathu labels every vial in the tapping-shed cupboard in his fine hand; the antidote is tagged 'Black gall, counter' and is a finger-length clay vial with a thumb-pinched wax stopper.
Chathu brings Neela a tin of warm jaggery-sesame sweets at dawn; she refuses to touch it (callback to F080).
The kennels lie under the oldest roof behind the cook-house and a shuttered well; there are forty-one cages of iron, holding animals including a deer, hare, mongoose and fox.
Chathu keeps the stolen antidote vial (hunters seized it); Ammu was recalled to the Resin House and rode through the night to arrive in the yard on the day of Neela's binding.
Chathu's left foot is uneven from an old break.
Vellan told Neela earlier 'Eleven for eleven. You've never missed.'
Devan told Neela about Muthu's quiet tell when he lies.
Neela learned to open the shed lock at fourteen, on a dare.
Neela and Ammu used the drain path through the Resin House wall as children.
Neela ordered Muthu to follow by cart at the second dusk, meeting her on the wood road; the cart is due at the Resin House gate at tonight's dusk, where Vellan will wait.
Neela now resolves to say the word herself, aloud, to someone before she is caged, without yet knowing the self-naming loophole.

Neela leaves Kettamala after the new-moon dusk, rides a night and a day, and is taken at the first dusk. Her order to Muthu: if she is not back by first light on the second day, put Devan in a cart and start up the wood road and meet her on it. Muthu leaves at first light of day two and reaches the Resin House gate at the second dusk, the dusk of Neela's binding. Replaces F242.

Chathu knows a cart is coming to his gate tonight and that Vellan will wait for it. Neela realises only she and Muthu heard the order, so the inside informant (F220) reaches Chathu fast; she recalls Muthu's stillness and 'I won't'. Chathu answers only 'A house pays its debts in news, child.'

Chathu recalled Ammu to carry the resin pot at dusk and to stand watch as a lesson after the covered scent-posts were found out. In the kennels her lips begin the tappers' verse 'the name given back' and stop.
Devan has held a river pebble in his cheek on the resin nights since the rampart (ch20 onward), not every resin night Neela has had.
Muthu brought Devan to the Resin House on horseback rather than by cart, and held the gatehouse arch against hunters while Devan's horse carried him into the yard.
Ammu hid a flat blade in her braid, lifted Pachan's key ring and stole the antidote vial from Chathu's sleeve.
Ammu learned the self-naming loophole at fourteen from a drunk old master and tells Neela the tappers' verse 'the name given back' refers to it.
Devan's ribs reopen when he strikes Vellan, and Neela feels a brief tearing along her own side while in shape without yet understanding it.
Ammu uses the jackal call 'tomorrow, I will find you' as her last signal before drawing Vellan and the hunters away.

The intake slip stitched to Neela's page survives the burning of the witness entry, unscorched. It reads 'Intake, sold at six years' with two further lines Neela cannot read. Chathu picks it up from the mud, covers it with his thumb, and keeps it. The witness entry burns while Chathu reads it aloud at dusk (after Neela's self-naming).
Before leaving the kennel, Ammu smears two fingers of resin from the pot on her own throat and wrists, so she can turn at sunset as a jackal. She leaves the pot in the straw.

Devan cannot stand after the antidote. He strikes the bear's shoulder once from one knee as its charge brings the shoulder to him, then pitches forward onto his hands. He does not rise again that night.
After Ammu's last cry, Neela in leopard shape smells jackal blood carried back on the wind; Ammu is dead and stays dead. Muthu survives the gatehouse fight, swearing hoarsely.
Ammu's body is found under a blackbark tree with a spear wound under the ribs, in a large coat from Muthu; she has a cord pouch holding a thumb of resin, which Neela keeps.
The torn resin scars at Neela's throat and wrists, from the forced resin in ch 27, appear as thin red welts on Devan's throat and wrists via the wound-share.

Ittan smells of clove oil and has a brick-red wax stain under his thumbnail, explained as rubbing clove on his wife's chest for her cough. His lead cart rides low on the axle with a roped chest under a tarpaulin.

Ittan arrives at Kettamala on the thirty-ninth day with five carts, the evening before the sealing. Devan lets him pass the gate without a search tonight, so he can be searched on sealing day under border custom.
Ittan says he proposed the match himself and is a matchmaker out of vanity.

Ittan arrives at Kettamala with five carts two days after Neela, Devan and Muthu ride in, the evening before the sealing. He was due days earlier and held at the lower waystation 'for an axle'; the charter sealing waits on the Keeper's own seal, so his lateness delays the closing. Devan reads the delay as Ittan waiting for news of a dead warden. Devan lets him pass the gate unsearched tonight so he can be searched on sealing day under border custom. Replaces the earlier thirty-ninth-day version.

Devan recognises Ittan's clove smell and brick-red thumbnail stain as the signature of genuine council wax (F050) but treats it as suggestive, not proof, because Ittan's wife's cough gives an innocent explanation and the Keeper's office holds a seal box by right.

Neela waters and feeds the forty-one kennel animals once and props the end door. Devan orders Muthu to take four men, a cart and fodder back to the Resin House in three days and weekly after while roads allow; Muthu agrees and says he will go himself. Cages stay shut because opening them would not undo the caging.

Neela's forced-resin scars were still open when she self-named, which is why they appear as red lines on Devan's throat and wrists. The wound-share carries wounds only: pain felt at a shared wound, such as her torn wrist pulling at his right wrist.

The false-bottomed teak chest in Ittan's lead cart holds thirty-six blank split-ash tally sticks wrapped in oilcloth, each with council wax bearing the dot-and-split mark, plus a hand-sized oilcloth tally book of about forty leaves recording dated sums and pass place-names.
Devan carries Asha's first token and his beeswax impression in his sleeve, and compares them to the chest's wax on sealing day; the dot-and-split mark matches.
Neela tells the court the slip was torn from a courier's papers by someone now dead, whom Devan declines to name.
Ittan is held in the padippura guardroom, and the warden's seal is an iron disc cut with a hill and a gate, worn by eleven wardens.

Border charter: if the Keeper's seal is found false, the warden may close the pass with his own seal alone, but the writ needs a witness of the warden's house marked beside the seal. Devan cites the single-seal line to Ittan in the courtyard before the search. Gopan names the witness requirement at the gate-tower.
Neela writes her name, with 'of Kettamala', as the household witness on the closing writ. The writ goes to Kodiyur, so her name is on a crown record.

Devan stood the five carts under the padippura roof overnight with Bhaskaran's men round them as a courtesy; Ittan's clerk came down at the middle watch with a lantern and was turned back, so the chest was never moved.
Ittan carried the 36 blank waxed tokens to wax passes under the widow's seal, where no clerk counts a seal box.

Devan reads Chathu's slip aloud, says only that his wife brought it before the new moon and that it came off a courier's papers, and names no source. He knowingly lets Muthu carry 'my wife brought me this'.
Neela's bound hand gripping the stair rail pulls at Devan's right wrist, within the wound-share limits of F265.

Neela has not turned tonight: she skipped resin so she could sit in the open west window as a woman. She holds Ammu's thumb of resin in a pouch, kept for ch31. Devan still holds the river pebble out of habit and sets it in his palm.

Devan says that on the night Neela put her fingers at the base of his skull (the marma point) and counted three breaths, he was awake, holding his sleeping breath too even, and that this was when he knew he could trust her. The scene is told undated, between her arrival and the storm.

Devan tells Neela he barred the shutters on the second dusk, pulled the sentry, kennelled the hounds and stopped Janu's stories so that no one else could become her witness, having decided before lifting the bar never to use what he had seen.
The guild tooth is a real leopard canine from the Resin House store, sewn into Neela's waistband; Devan pricks his thumb on it and a welt rises on her thumb.

Neela tells Devan the full terms of her twelfth contract and Chathu's threat, but offers no account of her earlier eleven contracts and mentions no lookout job; she does not know which fort the lookout job was.
Devan said 'I love you' to Asha in the kitchen the week before she died, and has said it to no one since until Neela.

Devan told Janu at the table, by day, that he was 'tired of leopards' to stop her stories; he never said the night-shape to Neela. He barred the shutters the second dusk, then removed the sentry a few nights later, then the hounds, and Janu's stories last.
Neela asks Devan to remarry her at noon tomorrow in the courtyard in front of Muthu; Devan warns that Muthu will report her words north in a grey-sealed letter, and she chooses to speak anyway.
Devan leaves a covered dish of rice and curd, a cup and a brazier-warmed cloth ready for Neela's dawn return; she never told him what the morning after a turning costs.
Chinna's wager on why the warden barred his shutters has no winner; Chinna keeps the stakes and guesses without asking.
Neela's vow publicly says she came 'sold' and names Raiu, Ammu and every living household member; she does not mention odiyans, Ittan or the guild before Muthu.

Ittan woke in the guardroom at the middle watch of the night after the vow and asked, through Unni, to speak only to the warden, saying he would tell Devan 'whose hand he is'. Devan held this back until Neela had turned back at dawn.
At first light after the vow, Neela sees Muthu cross the wet court to the guardroom door with a grey-sealed packet thicker than a month's letter.

The first Resin House fodder run was held by rain; the lower wood road drains in a day, though the Monkey Pass stays shut until spring. Muthu carries the cart (and Neela's cloth for Kirri) in three days. Devan rewarmed the dawn cloth at the brazier in the night.
Neela reads Muthu's quiet as a lie at the feast: he will report everything. She tells him to spell her name right, and knowingly trusts him with the cart carrying Kirri's cloth.

CORRECTED: The first Resin House fodder run was held by rain; the lower wood road drains in a day, though the Monkey Pass stays shut until the rains break (about four months, F020). Muthu carries the cart, with water and a clean cloth for Kirri's cage, in three days. Devan rewarmed the dawn cloth at the brazier in the night.

Near the middle watch Neela, in leopard shape, heard a low voice and a boot at the chamber door and took it for the watch changing; Devan rose, spoke three words and returned. He later tells her it was Unni with Ittan's request (F287).

Ittan's writing case holds an unfinished letter to his wife's physicians (boil the willow bark, she likes the window open in rain) and, beneath it, an oilcloth bundle tied with red thread holding Chathu's contract chit (a hide strip naming the warden's chamber, death by beast, before the pass closes) and the payment writ.

The payment writ is dated seven weeks before the wedding, payable to the Resin House on the warden's account, sealed in the queen's green wax with the sunbird; the seal matches the wedding-gift seal, including a small chip at the left wing tip.
Neela and Devan hide the oilcloth bundle under the third slat of the warden's chamber, telling neither Muthu nor the clerk.

Nine days into the rains Muthu returns from the Resin House fodder run: he laid the cloth in Kirri's cage, she lay on it with the anklet still on, and he saw Chathu on the cook-house step holding a black-covered book to his chest.

Ittan tells Devan through the guardroom grille that Muthu came at first light with a letter for the south. Devan took the grey-wax packet out unopened and locked it in the hall strongbox (key on his cord), because breaking the seal would tell Muthu he is read. It is still there nine days into the rains, and Neela decides to leave the wax whole.

Corrects F295: Neela and Devan hide the oilcloth bundle in a hollow in the shutter frame behind the housing of the third slat in the warden's chamber, not under a floor slat, telling neither Muthu nor the clerk.

Seven weeks before the wedding Devan wrote to the council that the raiders' tallies carried true wax and asked to see every seal register. The queen sealed the payment writ in response, before he had any suspect.
The warden's shutters are held on the wedding night only by an iron latch; the long teak bar hangs unused on its hooks.

The guild's pass-village watcher walks the hill edge each dawn reading fresh scent-marks; a first night with none reads as refusal and is reported to Chathu. This is why Neela must turn on the wedding night.
Neela deliberately presses the third slat to test whether the creak wakes Devan. She treats a sleeper's unchanged breathing as proof of nothing.

Captain Muthu sleeps in the lower barracks and wakes Devan for the dawn watch twice a week. The wedding bangle was made from a measure the council sent. There is a draught by the stair outside the warden's chamber.
Janu says it is the first time since Asha died that Devan has asked for food himself. This replaces F042 (eleven years).
Kannan carried the garland at the wedding.
The two guards on the upper wall pass each other at the far end every hundred and ten steps and turn on the same foot.
On the morning after ch3, Devan says to the shutters, 'The third slat creaks. I've never fixed it.' Neela finds the bar seated in its brackets as she left it and cannot read whether he heard her.
At first light at the end of ch4, both leaves of the warden's shutters are swung wide open, though Neela had left one leaf ajar; no face or lamp shows.

Devan opened both shutter leaves at the grey of dawn at the end of ch4 so Neela would see a way back that was neither guarded nor a trap; she turned back in the yard and came up the stair door as a woman after first light, so the bar was never lifted from outside that dawn. He goes to the kalari after first light.
In sunlight Devan sees that Neela's inner-wrist scars lie thick, layer over layer, meaning more than a decade of use, so she started young. The scars are on the inner wrist only.
Neela first lies about her scars on the terrace with 'a childhood burn' (before the second-week lie 'a fall from a cart', F200); Devan knows it is false.

Kunjan Chirayil kept the north warehouse in Kodiyur (smell of wet sacks and cloves); Bindu is Kannan's singing mother, learned from women at the well; Devan's father is dead and Devan spent two years at border school.
Asha came to the fort at nineteen and in her first month wrote every recruit's name and mother's village on a slate; Janu found Asha's body on the west stair.
Devan has Muthu pull the sentry from the rampart above the warden's window without reason, and leaves the shutter bar in place so Neela lifts it herself.

Before walking into the lower market, Devan watched Neela's meeting with 'Valli' for about a quarter hour from the shade of the tamarind wall (not the fish racks), until Muthu's laugh drew eyes and covered his approach. He saw the girl weigh the same measure twice and saw Neela's back go taut. He counts 'the coast girl who weighed twice' in his chain of suspicion: council, match, widow.
The council's seal dies were cut by the palace engraver, who is older than the queen (Muthu's remark).
The marriage settlement recorded in the writ is cloth, brass and four hundred panam.
Devan says he has laughed once before Neela made him laugh, 'a long time before' her. Muthu's next sparring request falls four days after ch 8's morning.
Chathu wrote Neela's page in resin-ink in a locked room on the day of her first turning; Ammu, then fourteen, held Neela's hand through that turning.

Neela has heard Devan's dawn drill (bare feet on packed earth, palm slaps on skin, sesame-oil lamp smell) in her sleep on mornings she slept, without recognising it. On the storm dawn she hears it from the west sill without seeing the pit, which lies below the east wall.

Devan states the stake behind his bargain: the raiders hit the coast villages before the pass shuts, the token-seller sells them his patrol road, and Raman's nine-year-old boy lost his father under the shelf.
Janu is the source of the damp-madness theory about the barred shutters (one of the fort's three theories in F103), and the kitchen ran a wager on it.
On a night without resin, at dusk Neela feels a faint pull at the throat and a burn in the resin scars, which passes if she breathes through it and leaves her human.
Devan, who left his sword on the floor in the morning (ch 15), sets it down again at night hilt toward Neela.
Corrects F153: Ammu has written four times (not eleven) to Kirri's address; Chathu answers only 'Kirri is where she wished to be, child.'

Revised wording of the second lie: Neela tells Ammu that Devan heard something pass behind him on the wall, never turned, said 'Go on, then' into the dark, and took it for the fort's notched ginger tom, which walks that wall every night. Ammu glances at Neela's hands, asks 'He didn't even turn his head?', then chooses to believe it.
On the first resin night with the pebble, Neela gives Devan Kannan's white pebble to hold in his cheek in place of his grey one; the grey one stays on the sill.
Neela's drawn-out tell when asked about the eleventh-step turn: she says 'I don't know', her lips move on a count and her thumbnail drags along her forefinger nail.
Neela counts the doors in every room she sleeps in, and says so to Devan; she answered to 'Seventeen' for twenty-one years.
Devan keeps a private tally of Neela's bare nights and chooses not to ask what ends at the new moon.

Before dusk Devan found the west stair lamps drained, not burned dry (wicks white, cups tipped): a sign the inside informant wanted the stair dark. He could not spare the stair-head pair, so he sent Raiu for oil with the chamber door barred from within. Replaces F229's 'run dry'. Neela, standing at the shutter listening for steel, hears the fight.

Neela's order to Muthu: if she is not back by first light on the second day, he is to bring Devan up the wood road after her, in a cart if he has to. Corrects F227's 'second dusk' and agrees with F244.
After the poison takes the Asha thought, Devan keeps only a fogged memory: a rolling torch and something dark at the wall. The rest slides away when he reaches for it, so the link stays closed.
Raiu's mother has been dead four years. Devan stood over Asha's body at twenty-six in the grey before dawn with Janu holding a lamp.
On the morning of ch25 one of Neela's nails had split; by the stable scene three have split to the quick. Devan notices it himself.

Neela's full order to Muthu (if she is not back by first light on the second day, bring Devan up the wood road after her, in a cart if he must) was given only to Muthu, out of Devan's hearing, in the passage outside the sickroom. In the stable she tells Devan only 'I've told Muthu what to do if I'm late.' Agrees with F244 and F245.

At the new-moon dusk the wall pairs were mid-change on the hour chain, so Devan sent Raiu for lamp oil rather than spend a stair-head man, and climbed the dark west stair alone as the only way to Neela's door. Refines F229 and F331.

The bear flees because Neela shouts 'Down! Both of you!' from the stair head and the two stair-head men come down with spears and lamps behind her; Vellan faces three blades and light. Neela's shout releases the men from Devan's 'Hold the head' order.
The poison's onset is physical first: numbness climbs Devan's left side and reaches his fingertips before it erases the Asha thought.

Revises F251: when Devan's ribs reopen under the strike, Neela in shape recognises at once that it is the wound-share Ammu described ('A cut on him opens on you'), and weighs it in the stay-or-follow choice: if she is speared, he bleeds too.
Chathu shouts 'The jackal has Pachan's key' (not 'my keys'), matching Ammu lifting Pachan's key ring.

Revises F264: Devan orders Bhaskaran's men (four men, a cart and fodder) to leave Kettamala the morning after the return, reaching the kennels within three days of Neela's watering, then weekly while roads allow. Muthu offers to go himself and Devan answers 'After the sealing. I want you at the gate.' Muthu carries the later run (ch 31).
Neela watches the sealing arrival from the west rampart above the warden's chamber window, where the pulled sentry used to stand; the wall bends toward the gate so she overlooks the padippura.

Devan stopped Janu's leopard stories at supper with Neela present (ch 9), then told Janu in the kitchen, by day, that he was 'tired of leopards'. He never said the night-shape to Neela. Order of his protections: shutters barred second dusk, hounds kennelled, sentry pulled, Janu's stories last (matches ch 4, 5, 9; corrects F282's order).
Devan says he said 'I love you' to Asha, badly, in the kitchen the week before she died, and to no one since until Neela.

The guild tooth is a real leopard canine from the Resin House store, meant to be left in Devan's wound; Neela wore it sewn in her waistband from Kodiyur. Devan pricks his thumb on it and a welt rises on her thumb.

Devan was wary of Neela for about eleven days. The moment he trusted her was the dawn at the kalari when she came down the north steps, put her fingers at the base of his skull (marma point), counted three breaths aloud, lifted her hand and told him his guard dropped on the left. He did not turn, and held his breath.

Neela asks Devan to remarry her at noon tomorrow in the courtyard before Janu, Muthu, Kannan and the household. Devan warns Muthu will report her words north in a grey-sealed letter; she chooses to speak anyway and will not tell Devan the words beforehand.

Devan tells Neela the first night he left the shutters shut on the latch, never barred, as his father kept them, and watched her climb to the sill; he barred them from the second dusk so no servant could become her witness.
Neela turns back in the yard at dawn and comes up the stair door with a saddle-blanket from the stable round her; Devan hears the rough wool drop before the bed creaks.

Devan's practical means for tracking Neela is reading her paw-marks in the wet laterite by the water trough each dawn. His truer reason for pulling the sentry is the witness rule: a sentry with a lantern two spans above the ledge could watch her turn and become a witness. Retire F064. F310 should say only that the wrist scars are the ones he sees.
The queen pays a death-gift to border soldiers' widows at harvest; Parukutty's debt falls due three months before it.
The salt factor adds a tally fee once a debt passes a month.
Four soldiers' widows on the wall rolls owe the salt factor. Devan says he will clear the other three by the new moon, and tells no one.
Unni is not much past twenty.
Ammu has a new nick across one knuckle, a planted detail for a later chapter to pay off or drop.
The Resin House punishes telling a member what the masters have not, which is why Ammu stops herself.
Ammu ties the pepper packet with a fisherman's double hitch, learned by both girls from a net-mender behind the sheds as children.
At the end of ch7 Neela decides to leave a written question about the 'way' under the meeting stone that night.
Ammu, 25, says Kirri (31) taught the younger girls their letters as the big girl and could not spell 'tide'.
Marma point a thumb's width below the base of the skull, called 'the door' by the old masters: a correct strike kills silently and leaves a man looking like he fell.

Devan has seven pale flat scars across the knuckles of his right hand and a thin white line across the base of the thumb, from years of hitting wood and stone. Neela reads them as the hand of a man who stopped hitting anything that hit back.

At first light after ch10 Neela sees Devan abed, though Janu says he rises in the last dark hour. She resolves to go to the kalari pit herself, human, tomorrow before dawn, and notes the pit is his ground and she would have one strike.
Neela's cover story includes having spent time at Kunjan Chirayil's warehouse, where one of two guards once stood a quay watch with a cudgel beside her (F107).
Devan has scars on his brow, in addition to the ribs seam (F193).
The sentry who walks the east wall above the kalari at dawn faces the hill and never turns round.
Neela has killed by marma strike in human form at least once before (the door strike 'once not in practice'), among her eleven completed contracts.
The pair of sentries on the east wall above the kalari at dawn face the hill and never turn round (refines F366; consistent with paired wall guards, F037, F306).

Neela notes a pattern: on nights she is out as the other one Devan lies abed until she is back, but on ch11's human night he rose in the dark and went to the pit. She wonders whether he is waiting for her; unresolved until the ch15 reveal.
Neela counts the three breaths aloud under her breath ('One', 'Two', 'Three') and Devan hears them, matching F347.

Revises F137: Neela drops the satchel on the patrol path because the warden broke a council-wax tally open in the hall (which she saw herself) and said one was not enough; this is a second. She has not seen Asha's token or note. A bag on the path also makes the camp read as raiders rather than a cat-kill, and she knows it tells Devan someone stood there before him.

On the ridge Neela counts the cost of skipping the stone a second night: an empty cup for Ammu, Valli absent from the gate, and Chathu's 'every day counts double' (F087). She chooses the narrows anyway.

At supper Devan shows only the coin's edge and says 'I won't answer that' when Muthu asks if it is loot; he does not voice his conclusion about Varanad silver or the second tally before the hall. Neela notes that he says less than he knows.

Chathu never struck a new intake: he learned which girl cried at night, left warm sweets by her mat and kept her fed and gentle for years before reading her page. Neela's reason for reading Devan's gift as patience.
On the no-resin night of ch 16 Devan's sleeping breath at first has no hitch; the catch then comes slowly, deliberately and evenly so Neela can count it.
Neela reckons the ache at nine or ten days by her count of rationed and lost resin nights; she expects the pass-village watcher to log no fresh posts at next grey, and Ammu to come asking by noon.

Order of Devan's protections as Neela rereads them: shutters barred from the second dusk, hounds kennelled from the second night, sentry above the window pulled a few nights on, Raiu at the stair head with the lamp unlit, Janu's story stopped with 'Not tonight, Janu' at supper.
Fort theories on the barred shutters: Bhaskaran's lads say damp-madness, Janu says shyness, Chinna runs the wager (corrects F322).

Ammu covered the second skipped night by taking Neela's spare day cloth from the cache under the second spur (F129) and rubbing it on each scent-post, so the posts read fresh with Neela's own scent. The cloth is spent and the cache is now empty. Replaces the 'jackal scent laid over hers' mechanism in F194.
Neela's three bare nights before the rain night (ch 16 to 18) were already logged by the watcher as gaps, as was the rain night of ch 21; Chathu's sweets were his answer to the three.

Neela knows the grove overlooks the warden's window and opens the shutters on purpose; she tells Ammu 'I knew it would be seen'. She also reasons that acting on the torn balance strip could expose Ammu to Chathu's caging.
Asha was found dead on the west stair within a month of finding the first forged token (six years ago).

Devan has known since boyhood in the kalari pit that Muthu goes quiet when he lies. On seeing Muthu hand a grey-sealed letter to a rider off post day, he recognises the tell, says nothing, and keeps the slip inside his shirt.
Neela counts nights to the rains, not the seal: the council seals the pass about three days ahead of the rains, so the seal is eight days off while her count is eleven.

A spring pass opens on two impressions: council wax on the token and the warden's gate impression beside it. Ittan's 36 pre-waxed blanks lacked the second; a widow holding the seal in trust, with the Keeper as adviser, could press it on all of them, and no gate roll counts a widow's impression. Replaces F273.

Before the search Ittan says no warden has opened a Keeper's cart in living memory, counting on Devan's eight years of never using power. At the middle watch the clerk came with a lantern and a pry-bar to the chest's ropes and was seized by Bhaskaran's men. Refines F272.
Chathu's slip is written in black, tacky resin-ink. Devan names no source, only that his wife brought it and it came off a courier's papers (F274). Retire F268.
Neela's name on the crown closing writ gives the crown a record it can match against unvouched rogue odiyans, which it is entitled to hunt.

Marriage-writ clause as read aloud in ch 29 matches ch 8: '...and the said wife, being lawfully wed, shall hold the pass-seal of Kettamala in trust from the hour of the warden's death, until the council shall name another in his place.'

A spring pass opens on two impressions: council wax on the token and the warden's gate impression beside it. Bhaskaran pressed the gate mark beside the dot-and-split tally he passed, so that wax was true. Ittan's 36 blanks carry only the council wax; no warden would ever stamp them, so they were meant for a widow holding the seal in trust, with the Keeper as adviser, who could press the second impression on all of them. No gate roll counts a widow's impression. Replaces F273 and the earlier F385.

Before the search Ittan says no warden has opened a Keeper's cart in living memory, counting on Devan's habit: eight years of a man who never struck first, and five of a warden who never once turned his power on anyone (Devan has been warden five years). At the middle watch the clerk came with a lantern and a pry-bar to the chest's ropes and was seized by Bhaskaran's men. Refines F272.

Chathu's slip is a single line in black tacky resin-ink. Devan, who had kept it since ch23 (F383), gave it back into Neela's keeping the night before sealing so that she would be the one to bring it forward in court.

Corrects F289/F291: Bhaskaran's men got water through to the Resin House kennels before the rain shut the wood road for a few days; the road opens again between downpours. Muthu's cart, with fodder, water and a clean cloth for Kirri's cage, is the second run, three days after the vow. The Monkey Pass stays shut until the rains break. Devan rewarmed the dawn cloth at the brazier in the night.

Refines F287: at the middle watch Devan sent Unni to Bhaskaran with the order that nobody enters the guardroom until Devan comes. He told Neela at dawn, after she had eaten, and she chose to wait an hour. Bhaskaran steps aside for Muthu, who enters with the grey-sealed packet, so Muthu gets the first word with Ittan.
Neela's vow states she has been given a number for twenty-one of her twenty-seven years; Janu calls Devan a man of thirty-two. Both ages are on the page before the dawn scene.

On the dawn of ch14, from the east terrace, Neela sees a single man come over the far ridge beyond the narrows and go down toward the dark scout camp while the patrol is bunched on the shelf; the scrub hides him and he does not reappear. She cannot act. No shot or horn follows.
Returning from the narrows in shape, Neela stops at the meeting stone in the pala grove and drags her cheek across the cup, a late scent-mark, before going to the cache.

Corrects F376: on the no-resin night of ch 16 the stone cup is bare for the third time (fever night ch 13, narrows night ch 14, tonight); the watcher's log would show a second refusal, since ch 11 was a human night.

Neela gives her plain six-inch guild knife to Devan, laying it on the boards on his side of the sword, hilt toward him, and says it is the only thing she has that is hers. She is unarmed afterward; later chapters must not show her carrying a blade without explanation (Devan may return it, or she may take another).

The 'dark rule' begins on the second night: in the dark she may ask him anything and he answers or says 'I won't answer that'. The ch17 'I won't answer that' about Asha's death is the first time he has said those words to her. Ch21's question game formalises this by limiting each player to one 'I won't answer' in total (F187).

Ittan has written Devan a kind letter every season for six years, beginning the winter Asha died (Devan was not yet warden for the first year). Devan reads the Keeper's letter aloud to Neela at lamplit dusk on the ninth day, after the post arrives.

Devan admits he was afraid for about a breath on the wedding night when he saw her turn, then afraid that she would look round. He says the shutters were held by the latch and she slipped it carefully so the third slat wouldn't ring.
Devan says that if he learns the buyer's name he would take it to the high court at Kodiyur with the seals and would not kill him.
Devan knows the names of the three keepers whose boxes carry the dot-and-split seal but does not tell Neela; he distrusts Muthu not at all and has no doubt of him.
Neela resolves to tell Ammu the seal boxes, the Keeper's letter and coming, the pass and the rider, but not that Devan is her witness.

Ammu says a torn strip from the carrier's balance sheet will be blamed on damp or rats until someone acts on the Keeper's name; then Chathu will ask who read that line, and only Ammu was near the satchel. Chathu's pressure on Neela this chapter is his message that every day counts double (F087), not a delivery of sweets.

Revises F342: Devan orders the first fodder run (four of Bhaskaran's men, a cart and fodder) to leave as soon as the wood road will take a wheel, within three days if the rain allows but liable to be held a day, then weekly while roads allow. Muthu offers to go himself; Devan answers 'After the sealing. I want you at the gate.' Consistent with F289/F291/F393.
Ammu's Valli cloth was shed at the cook-house corner; Muthu found it and laid it at the roots of the tree where she died, beside her resin pouch. Replaces the 'cached before dusk' detail.

Corrects F349: Devan tells Neela that on the wedding night the shutters were shut on the latch for the wedding guests and never barred, because his father never barred them and kept them open to breathe (consistent with F102, F121, F300). He barred them from the second dusk, kennelled the hounds that same night (F377), pulled the sentry a few nights after, and stopped Janu's stories last, so no servant could become her witness.

Corrects F347: Devan's day-eleven moment at the kalari (fingers at the skull, three breaths) taught him she would not kill him in the dark; it did not mean he trusted her with the name. He admits the ch15 silence-for-a-name bargain was a mistake and says he was wrong to make her pay for it.

Neela tells Devan the twelfth contract only and says there were eleven before it, which he may have one at a time if he asks; he says he will ask. Sets up the lookout-at-Asha's-death reveal in book 2.
Asha left unsigned notes ('Eat something.') on Devan's table, under his cup and inside his boots. Her parrot signature appears only on the notes found in ch 12.
Asha's body was found at the foot of the west stair, consistent with the stair newel and Janu finding her there.
While waiting for Neela's return, Devan carries his sword from the bedside floor to the window wall and replaces it hilt toward her side before she returns, so nothing in the room looks moved.

Devan keeps a carved box under the warden's bed; Asha's first token and her last note go into it on the evening of ch 12. F267 has him carrying the token in his sleeve on sealing day, so he retrieves it later.
As a girl Asha drew her parrot on the cistern-house walls until Janu scrubbed them off.

In ch 12 Devan tells Neela that Asha was his sister and, after, his second at the fort. Neela first hears it here. She also tells him, touching Asha's slate, that she learns every servant's name because she was 'a number, once, for a while'.
Asha's last note was found under the camphor block at the bottom of the chest; Devan withholds it from Neela (matches F115). The 'Thursday' of F114 is the seventh day in the draft.

Corrects F400: ch 12 is the first time Devan says 'I won't answer that' to Neela (about how Asha died), in daylight in Asha's room. The ch17 use is the first time inside the dark rule (the night-time ask-anything custom). F373's 'I won't answer that' to Muthu at supper in ch14 is to Muthu, not Neela.
Refines F417: Neela already knew the name Asha from ch 5 (F063, F313). In ch 12 she asks 'Is this Asha's?' and first hears from Devan that Asha was his sister and, after, his second.
Refines F110: Unni, now a guard of about twenty (F355), was the cook's boy who ran water to the recruits in Asha's time; Asha gave him a line on her slate. He was never a recruit.
Updates F114: Asha's sparring note refers to 'the seventh day' (Muthu's seventh-day sparring, F060), not Thursday.

Corrects F398: on the no-resin night of ch 16 the stone cup will be bare for the second time. Only the fever night (ch 13) was found bare by Ammu's jackal; the narrows night (ch 14) was marked late (F397) and passed. The watcher's log shows a second refusal, since ch 11 was a human night.

Token logic, replacing the two-impression wording of F385/F390: Bhaskaran's gate stamps only a stick carrying a clerk's number that matches a cart on the roll. Ittan's 36 blanks carry council wax with the dot-and-split but no clerk's number, so no gate would ever stamp them. Only a holder of the pass-seal (a widow in trust, with the Keeper as adviser) could number and stamp all 36 at once, with no roll to check against.

Muthu's quiet when he hesitates at the first cart is not his lying tell: Devan reads it as a man holding his breath between two loyalties. His objection about the queen's council and a writ is honest.

Clarifies F271: the closing is done in the gate-chamber directly over the padippura, under the same roof. Neela signs as the warden's wife, 'of Kettamala', on a border-law writ. She marks it as different from her earlier refusal to put her word before the queen as an odiyan's testimony.

Revises F426: the closing is done in the gate-chamber directly over the padippura, under the same roof. Neela signs as the warden's wife, 'of Kettamala', as household witness on a border-law writ that goes to Kodiyur. No earlier refusal to put her word before the queen is stated or implied. Devan sees her choice only in her hands. Ittan's tokens and the grey-sealed letter are said to go 'to the palace' or 'to Kodiyur', not north or south.

At the middle watch Ittan woke in the guardroom and asked, through Unni, to speak only to the warden, saying he would tell Devan whose hand he is. Devan sent Unni to Bhaskaran with an order that nobody enters the guardroom until Devan comes, and told Neela only at dawn after she had turned back and eaten.

Bhaskaran will hold Devan's order against anyone except Muthu, who is his captain. Devan cannot bar Muthu without telling the fort why. Bhaskaran steps aside for Muthu, who enters the guardroom with a grey-sealed packet thicker than any month's letter and gets the first word with Ittan.
Neela chooses to wait an hour at dawn rather than send Devan to Ittan, knowing Muthu may reach Ittan first.

Bhaskaran's men got water to the Resin House kennels before the rain shut the wood road; the road opens between downpours. Muthu drives the second run in three days with fodder, water and a clean cloth for Kirri's cage.
Chinna's wager on why the warden barred his shutters has no winner; she keeps the stakes and does not ask what was right.

Revises F297: after Muthu came out of the guardroom with the grey-sealed packet, Devan took it from his hand openly, in front of Bhaskaran and the yard, to lock it in the hall strongbox with the rest of the post for the spring rider. Muthu shrugged it off as routine. The wax stayed unbroken and Muthu believes his letters are unread. Ittan at the grille said only 'You've no idea whose hand I am, my friend' and then fell silent, the price of Neela's choice to wait an hour (ch 31).

Revises F299: seven weeks before the wedding Devan wrote to the council that the raiders' tallies carried true wax and asked to see every seal register. He realises now that those registers lead to Ittan's box, and the queen sealed the payment writ as he closed on Ittan.
Revises F434: Devan wrote to the council eight weeks before the wedding; the queen sealed the payment writ, dated seven weeks before the wedding, within days of his letter.
The guild contract chit is split in two: the buyer keeps one half, and the odiyan burns her half at the meeting stone when it is given to her. The chit Devan found is the buyer's half.
The queen's sunbird seal on the writ has a chip at the left wing tip, matching the cut wedding-gift seal. Devan recognises Chathu's mark from a seized courier's letter seen at border school.
Neela names the cost of Devan's 'Then I'll come': the fort, the garrison's trust and his office. Devan knows the queen holds Neela's name from the closing writ (F271, F388).
Asha grew up at Kettamala under Janu and took up her officer's post at the fort at nineteen; her recruit slate dates from her first month as an officer.
Devan's father was warden of Kettamala before him and wore the iron warden's seal; Asha once held it for a week as a joke and their father took it back crossly.
Saroja is a woman who sings at the well in one of the pass villages.
Ammu's Valli cover is a coast girl's blue cotton wrap.
The Resin House kennel aisle holds forty-two cages; Neela was put in one of them, and forty-one hold caged odiyans.
The forced resin in ch 27 was applied with a paddle by Chathu's hunters while Ammu held the resin pot, not by Chathu's own hand.
In the guardroom after the vow, Ittan's only request to Devan was that his wife's cough medicine be sent on.
In the margin beside three lines of Ittan's tally book is a tiny inked sunbird with folded wings, distinct from the queen's spread-winged seal; Neela cannot read it as guild shorthand.
Chathu enters every contract in the ledger against the subject's page, so Asha's contract entry is in the black book.
Ittan's tally book shows four payment slashes to the Resin House and a 'hook' mark meaning something delivered in return.
Neela always takes the east stair and avoids the west stair without stating a reason.
