Ammu's pouch held a thumb of resin of which two smears remain on the ninth day of the rains.

Plan agreed in ch 1: Neela spends the first of her two remaining resin smears on the night of ch 1 to run the wood road ahead as the other one; the second is kept for inside the Resin House. They take the wood road by the lower ford, half a day longer, because the ridge track is walked by the pass-village watcher.
Ittan's tally-book margin shorthand is copied from Resin House receipts, so Neela can read the counts and payments but not the masters' name marks.
The queen's warrant for Ittan bears the same green sunbird seal as the payment writ, including the chip at the left wing tip. Devan notices and says nothing.
The escort are called First, Second, Third and Fourth Guard. First Guard is a woman about Devan's age with a pale finger-long ridge on the inside of her left wrist.
Bhaskaran's horn code: one long note and two short means unarmed strangers at the gate, not many.
Rema takes the warden's chair in the hall. Janu quarters the escort in the south range. Rema's First Guard stands at Ittan's guardroom door beside Bhaskaran's men.
Rema grants an assize at Kettamala in three days, with Ittan heard as witness; she decides afterwards whether she carries out a traitor, a witness or no one.

Night before ch 2: the langurs' silence at dusk made Neela judge a night run too risky with strangers on the road, so she kept both remaining smears and did not turn. Corrects the reading of F451 for that night; the first smear is still unspent and the plan to spend it is deferred.
Neela deliberately takes the west stair into the hall in ch 2, reversing her habit of avoiding it (F449), so Rema will not notice which stair she uses.

First Guard's wrist mark is a single smooth, flat seam about a finger long, unlike Neela's thick layered ridges, and her throat is bare of scars; Devan reasonably reads it as a lamp-burn or rope burn. Refines F454.
Rema is 58 (harmonised; no 'about sixty').
Eravi's green clay-and-bark salve was left in thanks by Fourth Guard, who came to the dispensary for a blistered heel; it smells of scorched tamarind and pine sap. Neela keeps the pot.
Rema tells Neela she will be sworn at the assize as household witness to the closing writ.
Devan loosed the fourteen hounds at dusk on the day of ch 3; they had been kennelled through the nine days of rain.
Janu counts eleven servants' names Neela has learned beyond the household she was introduced to; the hall has eight pillars.
First Guard's hand goes to her own left cuff when she sees the binding on Neela's wrist.
Ittan's wife's cough medicine is a brown jar of honey-and-root syrup in his writing case, which she takes only warmed; Devan promises to send it on and offers to write to her physicians himself.

Ch 4 takes place on the second day after Rema's arrival: guardroom at midday while Rema and her escort are in the hall with the tally chest, the chamber scene that night, Unni's knock in the last dark hour before dawn of the third day.
Rema's moved execution rests on a wartime charter clause for a prisoner whose keeping endangers the pass; her escort had Bhaskaran's night men stand down at the guardroom.
Devan knows Muthu brought or carried something to Ittan (the grey-sealed packet, ch 31) and does not name it to Muthu, to keep him at the gate through the hearing.
Rema's four escort wear green sashes, which Unni calls 'the queen's sash'; it is the authority under which Bhaskaran's night men stood down.
The execution block is the wood-yard chopping stump, scrubbed pale, set in the main court; Rema's court-side objection is entered by Rema herself in writing since Ittan's clerk is held.
When Devan scrapes his knuckle on the kalari pit wall, a thin welt appears on the back of Neela's right knuckle through the wound-share.
Rema shuts herself in the south range with the tally chest from noon; her sitting opens at lamp-lighting on the day of the execution, after the escort has left on foot by the goat path.

Neela and Devan spar to two light touches with no marma. Neela scores the first on a guard Devan deliberately left open on the left, then the second on her own by earning it. Devan keeps her bandaged left hand out of the line and moves the pit lamp away from it.
Neela smells old nightbark on all four escort and reads them as guild hunters with forcing-resin come for her, because her name is on the crown closing writ.
First Guard says 'It passes' to Neela about her split nails at the padippura at dusk; Muthu does not appear to hear.
Kesu's grandson carries Ittan's cough-medicine jar and Devan's letter down the goat path at first light, since the pass is closed to carts.
Devan seals the letter to Ittan's household in plain black wax stamped with the warden's iron disc, and offers to pay from the account of Kettamala.

The Resin House ledger is two kinds of leaf sewn into one cover: front half plain-ink contract leaves (the 'contract books'), back half resin-ink pages. The contract leaves come loose at the stitching.
Neela has one smear of Ammu's resin left in the pouch, kept for the Resin House; the other was spent earlier. The ache is close: nails split and a night sweat.
Neela tells Devan what the intake slip behind her burned page says ('Intake, sold at six years', two lines unread) and that she wants only to read it alone.

Corrects F481 and the ch 1 count (F450/F451): by the evening of ch 6 Neela has exactly one smear of Ammu's resin left, kept for the Resin House. She spent the other two nights earlier, on the ridge, to see who walked the road. The ache is close: split nails and a night sweat, and she is past her last proper resin (no day count given).

Neela and Devan decide in ch 6 to ride for the groves that night at full dark, reaching the nightbark by noon of the next day. Devan will tell Rema at first light that he and his wife have gone to fetch the guild's paper. Neela will go over the compound wall as a woman, by a drain, and keep the smear for the night inside.
The front half of the ledger is plain ink in Resin House cipher (the contract leaves, which come loose at the stitching); Devan cannot read it, so Neela must read every contract aloud to him.

First term of the handover: contract leaves go to Rema, the high court or any bench; pages go back to their owners, read aloud by the holder by daylight. Devan adds that no clerks may be in the room, only the holder, the owner and whoever she chooses. Neela cannot yet promise to burn the back half.
Nightbark can be tapped at noon, and burns like fire only on bare skin.
Devan's letter to Ittan's household says the Keeper died at dawn by the queen's warrant, quotes Ittan's request that the window be kept open in rain, and names the account of Kettamala as payer.

The Resin House well house stands behind the kennel roof at the end of a flagged path: four posts, old tile, shuttered windows, plank door with an iron hasp, a farm lock and a teak bar in two brackets. Chathu carries the black book to it at dusk and returns without it.
The Resin House has eight hunters on the walls: two at the main gate, two at the drain, four under the wall. About forty members train in the yards.

Neela uses her last smear of Ammu's resin on the ridge at dusk to turn and scout the well house; Devan holds a pebble in his cheek until she is back at dawn. She now has the full flask of fresh resin from a stray nightbark on the ridge.
Neela cuts her right palm tapping the tree; a matching welt rises on Devan's right palm.
Pachan is tall, stooped, long-faced, in a grey wrap; he gave ten-year-old Neela a sweet when Chathu sat her at the table.
The Resin House kennels have hounds that stir at the cages and know every boot in the yard; they would scent an outsider on the flagged path to the well house.
Pachan held a net in the yard the day Chathu bound Neela three weeks ago and looked at his boots; he gave her the sweet at ten (consistent with F232/F493).
Devan proposes going in himself for the book and Neela rejects it: eight hunters, hounds and his unknown scent and boots on the flagged path.
The Resin House cook-house door is barred from inside once the long table has eaten; the east side of the compound is described only by wall and drain counts.
Bhaskaran's men who carried water to the Resin House kennels reported 'forty-odd' iron cages in a row with a door at each end; Neela confirms forty-one.
Neela scrapes her left shin on the scree in shape; a thin welt matching it shows on Devan's left shin, and he feels two sharp stings around the middle watch.

Neela's scouting reading: Rema's escort went down the goat path toward the lightning boulder and cart road, but the trail was lost on the scree in three days of rain; something heavier than a leopard went up the scree toward the shoulder the same night, leaving a long drag in fresh gravel.

Rema says Muthu has not missed a month in six years of letters to the queen's household; Devan realises six years matches the winter Asha died and that his captain's 'letters to his mother' were a lie.
Sergeant Bhaskaran has a wife and four daughters.

A man in a grey cloak from the queen's household approached Muthu the winter Asha died and asked for a monthly letter 'to keep the warden safe'. Muthu's mother is alive and writes to him on the ninth-day post, as F217 says.

The thick grey packet Devan locked away holds Muthu's month-report on two leaves plus the household's order slip ('Say nothing, and your wife is kept') in a clerk's round hand. Ittan read the slip and handed it back, and Muthu enclosed it with his own letter.
Muthu keeps a small brass post-key on a cord at his belt for the gate's post chest; Devan takes it so all post passes through Devan's hand.

Muthu's letters to the household never mention where Devan lays his sword, yet Vellan knew (F214/F220), which points to an informant who has been in the warden's chamber. Neela and Devan conclude it is not Muthu. This is clue C11.
The raid on the Resin House goes in on the dark of the moon, with Devan leading the ridge party and Muthu holding Kettamala with Rema inside the walls.

Muthu resealed the grey packet in the guardroom with the grey stick he carries, after Ittan read the slip and handed it back and Muthu enclosed it with his own letter. Muthu's letter reports sealing day: Ittan's carts searched, the Keeper held in the guardroom, the warden's wife signing the closing writ; Rema's arrival is not mentioned.

The slip 'Say nothing, and your wife is kept' reached Muthu by a lathered household rider on the off post day before sealing day (the ch23 rider), with a standing order to put it in the Keeper's hand if he were ever held. Muthu read it, delivered it to Ittan in the cell, took it back, and resealed it with his letter.
Devan cites Rema's written objection to Ittan's execution as proof she records against the crown, and trusts that she records, not that she is loyal to him.

Corporal Kandan of Mathoor, past thirty with a scar through one brow, was Raiu's comrade; his mother Kalyani has been lame in the left leg since spring. He refuses to be 'known' by Neela and stays unwon.

Garrison men Neela learns: Vasu (mother keeps ducks at Kalladi), Sankaran (mother returned to Neerattu), Kuttan (cannot write; Neela writes his mother a line). Fourteen men in the barracks at the noon meal.
Neela keeps her barracks name list in chalk on a broken roof tile, modelled on Asha's slate; Devan sees it and nods once.

Neela has walked round the west stair newel since her first days at Kettamala, before Raiu died, and cannot say why; she blames Raiu only afterwards. The fort's talk says Devan bowed to Rema at Ittan's execution.

The eleventh step of the west stair rings hollow; at the side of the stair, low in the wall, is an iron drain grate with file-bright bolts and no rust, newer than the stair by years. The long way up is the east stair and wall-walk, eighty-one steps by Neela's count.

Corporal Kandan tells Neela he will give Rema a statement for her roll about the bride learning every man's house and the warden bowing; Neela knows a roll can feed a crown record of her. She chooses not to tell Devan, so Kandan is not moved and made a martyr.

Neela's left hand is bandaged (F475) and her right palm carries a three-day-old scab from the nightbark tree (F492). In ch 10 she works and throws with the right hand; Chinna's ladle strikes her right knuckles and a welt rises on Devan's right knuckles over his old scars.

Neela already knew the eleventh step rings hollow and that she walked wide of the newel since her first week; she told Devan 'I don't know' (F328). Only the file-bright bolts on the grate are new to her, and Janu's matching curve frightens her.
Parukutty's daughter is named Minnu (six) and her son Chandu (nine).
Rema pays Parukutty's early death-gift as twelve new silver coins, more than the salt-factor debt plus tally fee; Rema writes the receipt herself because Ittan's clerk is held.

The widow's coin and the scouts' coins share a die flaw: the lowest leaf of the pepper sprig is doubled, and they weigh the same to a grain on the granary pepper scale. Neela trades a worn panam for one bright coin.
The black book is kept on a dry ledge cut into the Resin House well shaft a few man-lengths down, above the water. Neela and Ammu dropped a pebble down it at eleven and noticed the wrong sound.

Plan: Neela goes over the east wall as the leopard, quiets the hounds, opens the drain, and lifts the well-house bar; Devan comes over at the ridge party's signal, goes down the shaft on a rope, and holds the book from then until Neela turns back at dawn. Devan's rule: if he begins reading a page for any reason, she must stop him.
They ride from Kettamala at first light on the raid day and reach the ridge above the Resin House by dusk; the last night in the warden's chamber is the night before the raid.

Neela's first contract (at nineteen) was Raghu, a collector who worked for a Kodiyur port enforcer on the quays behind the pepper warehouses; he had crippled a boatman's eleven-year-old son's arm with a stick. She killed him with a marma strike at the base of the skull in a lane behind the fish market, was sick in a drain, then went back and ate.
The first contract leaf carried a small hooked mark in one corner, which Chathu said was for the accounts.

Neela and Devan agree the ledger-veto bargain: whoever holds the ledger and begins to read a page at night for any reason, the other takes it from their hand and they let go, no reasons given; each swears it twice. Pages may be read only by daylight, aloud, before the subject.
Neela remembers some of her other contracts: a magistrate with a bad knee, two sisters in a coast house, a boy on a river barge and his buyer.
A small door in the wall beside the warden's chamber hearth, which Neela counts as a door and has found no use for.

Ledger-veto signal agreed in ch 12: on the raid night Neela is a leopard and cannot take the book from Devan's hand, so if he begins to read a page she closes her teeth on his right wrist, a hold that does not break skin (a bite would open on her too). He then shuts the book and sets it on the well curb without giving a reason.
Neela's stated fear: Chathu keeps intake slips with the pages, and she could turn other women's leaves by night hunting hers. If Devan refuses the bargain she will not go over the Resin House wall.

Bhaskaran leads the eight-man ridge party. Vasu, Sankaran and Kuttan ride in it. The men camp three hundred paces back at a cairn on the wood road with shuttered lanterns, under orders that nobody climbs above the stones, so none can witness a turning.

Agreed raid signal: Neela gives two sawing calls a count apart once the drain is open and the well-house bar is up. Devan moves on the second call and goes over the wall only for the shaft, wrapping his palms against rope burn.
Neela told Devan on their second night together that the worst part of the shape is that nobody speaks to you. In ch 13 he talks to her while she circles the camp.
In shape Neela smells old bear musk, about two days old, on the wind off the Resin House.

The children's drain path is a culvert behind the midden, eleven body-lengths long, where the wall's footing washed out; it ends in a grate shut with an iron pin on a short chain. Neela leaves the pin on the stone and the grate ajar.
The well-house door's hasp staple is set in rotten post wood; Neela pulls staple and farm lock out whole with one claw, then lifts the teak bar with her teeth.
In the shaft the iron box with its fist-sized padlock hangs from a chain over a beam pulley, a few man-lengths down above the water.

Resin House night watch now includes odiyans in shape among the hunters on the walls; Neela notices and files it as a question for later. Pavi, 24, is an otter with a white chin and a curled, old-broken forepaw, who came at eight; Neela braided her hair the night before her first turning.
A hunter's pole-hook clips Neela's ribs; a shallow welt rises on Devan's side, over his old seam, and he says 'Then it's mine.'
The Resin House hounds lie cowed and silent because of the two-day-old bear musk across the yard.
Vellan in bear shape drags a hind leg: a drag and a step.
The black book's iron box was riveted at the hinge side; Devan sheared the hinge rivets with the pry bar, leaving the padlock shut. The book is wrapped in greased cloth.
Neela is raked by the bear: claw lines across her back and flank. They show as shallow welts across Devan's back from left shoulder blade to right hip, plus the hook welt at his ribs from ch 14.

Bhaskaran's party was ordered to come at the House's alarm horn or at the lamp signal; a hunters' horn on the east wall sounds after the bear roars. Ten men come in: eight over the east wall with lamps and two through the drain grate.

Devan holds the book up to stop the hunters. Chathu offers to 'write the rest off' and then flees on foot to the wood with Vellan (still in bear shape, struck on the shoulder by Devan) and the hunters, who carry off the stunned one.
Devan orders Bhaskaran's men to face the gate at dawn and never to say what the animals are.
Devan carried Neela's day cloth and the leaf packet of cold rice and curd inside his coat from the ridge; he holds the cloth out behind him with his back turned while she turns back.

The Resin House ledger's front half opens with a tidy index in Chathu's hand (year, place, leaf). The first heading is 'Released': one leaf listing twelve names, each with a tick and the margin note 'Kennel, N'. Kirri's is 'Kennel, nine'.

Kennel doors carry wired tags with painted numbers (white paint). Kirri's cage tag reads nine; Neela saw it in ch 14 and did not read it. The numbers follow the kennel roll, not position in the aisle.
Vellan's ledger number is Thirty. His entries run to thirty-six contracts with no 'released' beside any. Neela tells Devan this and turns past them unread.

Chathu files contracts bought by Ittan in a separately sewn 'Keeper's' quire marked with the hooked mark. Asha's leaf reads: 'The cold month, six years gone. Kettamala, the warden's sister, the west stair. Buyer, the Keeper. Hand, Thirty. Lookout, Seventeen. Closed. Paid in full.'

Neela remembers being unblindfolded at the foot of the west stair with a shuttered lamp, told to open it twice if anyone entered the court below. No one came. She counted to three hundred and ten, was blindfolded again and walked out.

The last quire of the ledger's front half is stitched round all four edges in green thread under a lump of green wax pressed with the queen's spread-winged sunbird. Devan refuses to break it; Rema or the high court will.

Revises F552: Chathu files contracts bought by Ittan in a separately sewn 'Keeper's' quire marked with the hooked mark. Asha's leaf reads: 'The cold month, six years gone. Kettamala, the warden's daughter, the west stair. Buyer, the Keeper. Hand, Thirty. Lookout, Seventeen. Closed. Paid in full.' (Devan's father was warden then, F440; Devan became warden five years ago.) Devan says aloud, 'My father was warden then.'

Neela was called to Chathu's room twelve times, once before each of her own twelve contracts including Devan's. The lookout night at Kettamala came with no summons: a hand on her shoulder in the dark and a blindfold.
Devan carries Kannan's white pebble in his belt pouch at the Resin House and puts it in his cheek at dusk of ch 17 although Neela took no resin, to slow his own words while angry.
Devan made his slow open-hand drill at twenty-five, the winter after the ford, ending with two fingers stopped a hair short of the post.
Pavi offers a clay pot of green salve; Devan has it left on Chathu's desk for Neela. He also sets a brass water pot spout-left by her mat and has the mat moved away from the door.
Devan decides not to hand the Keeper's quire to Rema until he has heard all eleven contracts, and will not lie to Rema about the lookout leaf.
Thilak is a Resin House member, 41, a tapper before he was an odiyan and a member for twenty-two years; he brings Neela the master's tea (Chathu's ginger blend) and calls her 'Master' without irony.

Neela writes the members' names on a plank from the carpentry shed in lamp-black: thirty-one real names, nine blanks. Twenty-two (a girl) asks whether her roll names her; Neela says she cannot give it yet because giving a name means reading the entry aloud.
Sample intake-roll names glimpsed by Neela: Thulasi, daughter of a salt-boiler, Pazhayangadi; Kumaran called Kuttu, a ferryman's son.
Neela keeps the Kettamala spearmen's spare spears for the grove pairs; Devan leaves eight men (Bhaskaran among them) and rides out with six.
Neela has kept a torn slip, her own page-slip, on the master's desk.
Devan splits the ten Kettamala men who came in at the raid (F545): four ride out with him, six stay at the Resin House, Bhaskaran among the six.

Neela tells Devan she will vouch for the forty as the Resin House under her own name; Devan answers that a vouched house has a master and the crown will write her name beside forty. Neela accepts that cost.
Neela's elder-sister contract (the third) involved two coast-house sisters; the elder kept bees. Twenty-two's intake name has four syllables.

Devan wore the brass post-key on a cord at his own neck since taking it from Muthu (ch 9 of book 2), and returns it to Muthu in the gate chamber over the padippura, asking him to bring anything he cannot carry to Devan first.

Eravi asks leave to ride up the wood road to 'a tapper I know' for willow bark and poppy, leaving at first light with Sankaran as escort as far as the ford, back in two days; his cuff smells of the green salve. Devan does not ask the tapper's name.
Devan's patrol order sends six men under Corporal Kandan to walk the lower narrows to the shelf and back before dark, to find who the scouts' mirror signalled; Kandan's men initially refuse, then go.

Devan reaches Kettamala at noon after riding through the night, and the assize sits at lamp-lighting that day. He leaves on the grey mare after the welt opens. Rema counts three 'I won't answer that' answers that day and notes Neela's absence from the witness bench.
Two hunter arrows hit Neela's left ribs: a scoring graze at lamp-lighting (the welt Devan felt in ch 19) and a second, bleeding graze at dawn in the grove. Both from the wood, one shot each.

The tin of warm jaggery-sesame sweets was left on the Resin House gatepost by hunters during the night, still warm, with Chathu's note ('The book is not yours to carry. Bring it home, and the account closes... Come home. C.') and Neela's intake slip beneath.

The ledger's key is a grid of cipher letters against plain ones at the back of the contract leaves, with a leaf of masters' marks: sunbird alone means 'by leave', hook means delivered, slash means paid.

Ittan's tally book has two columns: his own extra passes (hook) on the left and sunbird-marked 'by leave' passes on the right. The oldest leaves are copied in brown ink from an earlier book. 'Nellimala. Second harvest. Two boats of Thurai men, the coast road to the foot of the pass. By leave.' is twenty-one years back.
Neela's birth name is Indu, of Nellimala, on the coast side of the Monkey Pass, a day below Kettamala; she will keep both names.
Neela carries Ittan's oilcloth tally book in her wrap since the night they took the ledger.

The leaf under the sweets is the Resin House roll leaf from which Neela's torn desk slip (F565) was cut; it has fastening-holes along one edge, two lines in the members' cipher and two in the masters' cipher. It is Chathu's down payment, not the desk slip.

Neela reads members' cipher already; the masters' cipher and marks are on a separate key leaf at the back of the contract leaves, found two nights before ch 20. Only some lines of Ittan's right-hand column carry the sunbird mark.

Chathu's note promises the rest (who sold her, every roll he did not burn) if she comes home, and threatens Thilak, who walks the north tapping path at dusk. Neela has Kuttan fetch Thilak inside the tapping shed compound before dark.
Neela warmed-water care: Devan warms the cloth water because she once told him in the dark that cold water on open skin made her teeth hurt.
The grey mare favours her off hind; Neela knows her by the sound on the wood road.
Neela erred by leaving the east grove pair standing through the dawn change after a day and a night awake; the second arrow came at that change.
Neela decodes the masters' lines of the roll leaf at the master's desk, letter by letter against the key grid, after matching its torn edge to her desk slip.

The two members'-cipher lines on the roll leaf read 'Intake' and 'Sold at six years'; the two masters'-cipher lines give 'Indu, of Nellimala, coast side of the Monkey Pass' and 'Village burned the second harvest'.
Chathu offered a twelfth tin of sweets in the kennels, which Neela refused (F234); this is the thirteenth tin counting that one.

Neela asks Devan to stand a night with Bhaskaran's six at the groves before they leave; he shows them the east pair's blind ground under the tallest trunks, and she leaves Bhaskaran, the six and Pavi holding the shed with Thilak kept under a roof.
Devan writes the court case in plain words in his own hand while Neela reads the cipher aloud; Neela carries the ledger back to Kettamala in her saddlebag.

Eravi asks Neela how many members the Resin House holds and on which day she will read the pages back, though she has told only Devan, Pavi, Bhaskaran and Thilak of a reading day. She files it unanswered.

Janu fell asleep at the kitchen fire waiting up with Asha's supper warm on the night she died, woke at the cock, and found the body when she went out for water in the grey. She has kept ten paces from the stair foot for six years for this reason; in ch 23 she crosses them for the first time.

The iron grate under the eleventh step is the outer face of the old slop-gate postern, which opens on the outside path under the wall; the old gate was wood strapped with iron, locked with a fist-sized lock and barred, and is now replaced by new iron with file-bright bolts. Gopan did not make or order it, and Devan gave no order for it.
Gopan says nobody but the physician (Eravi) has ever carried the postern key: not Gopan, not Bhaskaran, not Janu.

Gopan missed the refit of the postern because the lip of the eleventh step hides the grate from above, a thick bank of lantana covers the outside path, and he lay a month in the fever year while the sergeant's men kept his rounds.
The old fist-sized lock hangs on the new iron postern door; the same key still fits it, so only the physician's old key opens the new door.

Eravi came to Kettamala twenty years ago at forty from a coast clinic; a tapper's widow sold him cheap Resin House poppy and willow bark, paid for in news of weather and sickness. Six years ago a big gentle-spoken guild man asked him to open the old slop-gate postern for one night; Eravi wrote Asha's death up as a bear and kept the key.

Eravi gave the guild three pieces of news since the wedding: the sword hilt toward Neela (seen while sitting by Devan's sickbed), the cart order overheard in the passage outside the sickroom, and the drained west stair lamps. He was told the lamps were only meant to frighten.
Devan holds Eravi in the gate chamber over the padippura, under Bhaskaran's man, writing a dated account for Rema.
Bhaskaran is at Kettamala; his men under Vasu (mother keeps ducks at Kalladi) were left at the Resin House with Pavi, and Vasu is the rider who comes off the wood road at first grey.
Devan and Muthu agree he will ask Muthu straight in future and Muthu will say 'I can't' when he cannot answer.

A note in the salve pot, a week before tonight, asked Eravi how many the Resin House holds and on which day the pages go back. Eravi asked Neela (ch 22), got no answer, and wrote that he did not know; Chathu does not have the reading day.

Devan orders Bhaskaran to send his best rider to Vasu at the Resin House at first light, because the wood road cannot be ridden by night; the horse is saddled in the yard when Vasu arrives first, so the warning is too late.
Bhaskaran rode back from the Resin House with Devan that morning; Vasu leads the six men left there.
Rema's assize is still sitting on the morning of ch 25; Devan leaves mid-session and Rema has the court note his absence.
Neela put off the first reading of the forty's pages until after the assize; Devan asked once, on the ridge road, that she read them sooner, and she gave a good reason.
Bhaskaran and eight Kettamala spearmen ride with Neela and Devan to the Resin House; Pavi and Vasu's six are outside the wall in the lee of the tapping sheds.
Chathu holds the nightbark groves and threatens to burn them with a torch at the nearest grove and a fire in the oil store; the forty's pages are in Neela's saddlebag with the ledger.
In human form Vellan walks with a hitch on the left leg, a drag and a step, matching his bear-shape drag.
Chathu, first witness at every one of the forty's turnings, will cage from the wall any of the forty who refuses to hunt Neela and Devan after the forced turning.
Chathu's hunters hold the wood road behind Neela's party, so there is no riding home before dawn.
Corrects F606: Bhaskaran, eight spearmen, Devan and Neela ride in (eleven); five Kettamala men and Pavi are outside the wall, since Vasu rode to Kettamala.
Madhavi is one of the forty (replaces a name that echoed a village).
Meenu is one of the forty, a member who cried at the roll leaf; at the Resin House wall she is pressed against the stone.

Rema called the assize at first grey on the morning of ch 25; Devan, Neela, Bhaskaran and eight spearmen leave within the hour and reach the Resin House late afternoon with the sun a hand above the trees.

Neela counts thirty-nine of the forty on the wall; Pavi is outside with the five Kettamala men. Neela rejects a daylight reading at once: a full reading would announce every night-shape to the hunters, and Chathu, first witness at every turning, can still cage regardless.
Neela's flask of resin is in the Resin House tapping-shed store, boxed with every member's ration and tagged, because she put it there the week she took the House so no one could say she kept more.
Neela binds the forty pages (without Vellan's) flat in oilcloth under her wrap against her ribs; the bound ledger body and the lamp ride on Devan's canvas pack.
Devan sends Bhaskaran and the Kettamala spearmen east along the ridge toward the old cairn camp, with orders not to look at the wall after sunset, so none of them witness a forced turning.
Pavi tried the drain grate at noon before Neela's party arrived to reach the flask in the store; it was pinned again and two hunters sat on it.
Neela's flask is in the store inside the Resin House wall; Neela has no bad ankle, only the ache.
Devan sends Pavi and the five Kettamala men from the sheds east with Bhaskaran's party.
Bhaskaran salutes at Raiu's pyre.
Thulasi (a salt-boiler's daughter, from the intake roll glimpse) is among the forty Neela calls by name.
Ammu's blue Valli cloth and cord pouch, weighted with a flat stone, still lie at the roots of the blackbark tree where she died.
A fox-sized animal bites Neela's left calf and another bites Devan's left thigh; each bite opens identically on the other through the wound-share.
Neela promises Twenty-two that her roll will be read at noon in the sun, only if she wants it, with whoever she chooses present.

Wound-share in ch 27: an original bite bleeds on the one bitten; on the partner it rises as a hot, shallow, weeping welt that does not open. Neela's calf bite bleeds and a welt rises on Devan's left calf. Madhavi's bite on Devan's thigh is a real wound and a welt rises on Neela's thigh.
Madhavi (brindled animal, one of the forty) does not break off when named, closes on Devan's thigh and draws blood; Neela weighs the packet and chooses not to read her page, and Madhavi lets go.
Chathu's plain-ink line on Vellan's contract leaf, 'Thirty. Release not to be granted. Sell to the crown when spent', has been written since Vellan's third contract.
Thilak brought Neela tea for nine days at the Resin House.
Twenty-two's intake name is Kamalakshi; her page is read in the shed with Pavi present.
Thilak's ledger number is Four and his shape is boar. Kuttu is Kumaran, a ferryman's son. Thulasi is a salt-boiler's daughter of Pazhayangadi.
Vellan's intake roll reads 'a joiner's son, of Venmanal, sold at nine'.
Kirri's ledger number is Twelve and her intake roll reads 'Kirthika, a boatwright's daughter, of the coast, sold at five'.
Muthu brings thirty garrison volunteers against Rema's posted order, burns his unsent grey-wax month letter in the gate fire-basket, and keeps his men facing the road so none witnesses a turning.
Chathu is taken to Kettamala on horseback by Muthu's men, with a gag cloth for after dusk until dawn, so he cannot say any shape aloud.
The forty ride east to the old cairn camp, held by Bhaskaran's men, to wait until the court has spoken. Each took a season's flask. Pachan keeps kennels and groves with no one rationing resin.

The cut-away back half of the ledger has many stubs of leaves cut by a clean blade, each marked in the margin with a tiny sunbird with folded wings, echoing Ittan's tally book. Neela counts them twice and tells no one yet.
The reading of all 41 caged odiyans' pages is done cage by cage that afternoon; each page is left in the straw. Cages stay shut.
Before the public reading Neela sends Muthu's two guards out to the apron to face the road; Thilak and Kuttu guard Chathu on the cook-house step, so only the forty and Devan hear the pages.
Pavi rode back from the cairn camp at first light on the reading day and is present in the yard.
Unni rode with Muthu's thirty and watched him write his last month letter; Rema's escort had already left by the goat path.
The Resin House kennel aisle has forty-two cages in a single row, forty-one filled. Neela reads eighty-two pages in the day: the forty, Vellan's, and forty-one kennel pages.
The assize hearing in the hall is held at noon, two days after the return from the Resin House, in daylight so Chathu is ungagged.
Rema keeps a second sealed case tied in green thread at her feet, unopened during the assize; she glances at it when Devan mentions the seal.
The night before the assize Devan told Neela he would put the lookout leaf before Rema himself, bearing the cost; she did not answer.
Kandan called Neela a witch to her face at the barracks door the week Raiu burned.
The queen's second writ is dated eleven days before Ittan's execution and bears the sunbird seal with the chip at the left wing tip; Rema was told to open it only if Neela answered yes under oath.
Rema tells them she will record that they left within three days and will not record where they went.
Muthu swears to hold the seal for the border and the villages, not for the queen's household, Devan's house or his own.

Janu's unfinished leopard story ends: the leopard, driven from the village, comes back to the hill's edge every night; they keep the door and a lamp open and she walks in. Devan stopped the stories because he was not sure Neela was ready to hear that ending.
Neela's sleeping/lying breath has a small catch at the ninth count of a long breath; Devan's is at the third part of his. Neela counts his hitch every morning as proof he is still there.
The wound-share carries pleasure as a warmth as well as hurt, on a night they are together.
Forty riders on borrowed horses wait in the road below the padippura at dawn; Bhaskaran's horn (one long, two short) announces them.

On the last night Neela feels the dusk pull at the open shutters (throat burn, ten counts, passes) and names the cost: she has no resin of her own for the road, the forty hold the season's flasks, and each bare night counts toward the ache.

Rema looked at the green-sealed last quire of the ledger's front half, said a seal the queen laid on was not hers to break, and left it with Devan; it travels in his pack, and whether to open it is now Neela and Devan's choice. Neela thinks it holds the queen's sealed contracts with the Resin House, possibly tied to the folded-wing sunbird stubs in the back half.
Neela's own resin flask went with the season's flasks given to the forty; she has none for the road.
Devan owns to Janu that he stopped her leopard stories so the kitchen would stop looking at the bride's window; this supersedes F651's reason.

The pepper hunters' shelter above the tree line is a stacked-stone hut with a turf roof, one low door and a hearth, used in the dry months by wild-pepper cutters; Kesu's grandson drew the route on a tally stick.

Thilak's inventory: forty-one season flasks (forty plus a spare Pavi carried), nine hooked tapping knives, and a small copy of Pachan's grove map showing the north slope and three trees that run best at noon. Neela refuses the spare flask.

The sealed last quire holds one sheet headed 'Sold to the crown' listing thirty ledger numbers with years and sums in panam, each with a folded-wing sunbird in the margin, and behind it the cut stubs of thirty leaves.

Vellan holds his own page (read to him by Neela earlier) and walks up unscented by resin; he says the queen's night-guard numbers thirty-one, that four escort guards crossed the shut pass by the goat path (he taught two of them), and that the queen witnessed each guard's first turning. He does not name any night-shape aloud.
Vellan gives Kamalakshi a carved wooden bird; she keeps it but says she has not forgiven him. Devan leaves a folded cloth beside him.

The sealed last quire holds only the single 'Sold to the crown' sheet (thirty ledger numbers, years, sums, folded-wing sunbird in each margin). The thirty cut stubs remain in the ledger's back half (per F638), each carrying its ledger number in the margin beside a folded-wing bird; Neela lays them beside the sheet and every one matches. Corrects F661.
Vellan says the queen's night-guard numbers thirty (not thirty-one); 'I'd have been the thirty-first'. Corrects F662.

The pass-village watcher's scent-post log goes to Chathu's cell and then to whoever opens his post, the queen's household; the next entry goes in at the new moon, after which anyone can follow the forty's trail.
Neela's lamp-black plank of the forty's names travelled up the hill lashed to a packhorse, carried by Kuttu's insistence.

At the shelter Neela and Devan carry the plank out to the forty and each speaks a two-line vow before them: she to read the thirty their pages by daylight and be no one's master; he to stand in the door and not close it.
Kamalakshi's age is not given in this chapter; the earlier 'twenty-two' echo of her ledger number is removed.

The queen's night-guard hide their throat scars under a lime-and-ochre paste; the wrist scars are real and hidden by cuffs. This reconciles First Guard's bare throat and smooth seam (F460) with the odiyan scar rule (F014).

At the shelter Neela gives the forty a standing vote to remove her from keeping the ledger and plank, no reason needed. Devan states aloud he stands at her back, not as her wall, and that he goes where the vote sends her. Replaces the vow in F668.
Neela counted the cut stubs twice at the Resin House and told only Devan; she crossed the Monkey Pass once as a child, at six, not by choice. Corrects ch 32 draft wording.
The Kettamala garrison wears grey.
Devan first walked the goat path at nineteen, on a dare, and it took the skin off his knees.
Rema's escort strung ropes at the three worst places on the goat path, in the dark, on the night they climbed to Kettamala.
Eravi was thrown out of his coast clinic for a drunken wrong dose before he came to Kettamala at forty.
A member of the forty with ledger number Thirteen has a boar night-shape (as does Thilak, Four).
Muthu's mother told him about his quiet lying tell when he was nine.
At the assize Chathu testified by daylight that the Keeper bought the warden's sister: four slashes paid, one hook delivered, 'the service was a bear's'.

Rema recorded for the high court that Asha's murder and the forged pass sales were one conspiracy bought by the Keeper. She entered Asha by name: 'daughter of the late warden of Kettamala, officer of the border, aged twenty-two. Killed under contract.'
Neela read the lookout line aloud in the assize under her own name and number, and answered 'Yes' under oath when Rema asked whether she is an odiyan.
Rema offered that if Neela left alone by sunset she could record that the warden harboured no unvouched odiyan. Devan refused aloud before the hall and had it entered that he harbours his wife.
Devan unhooked the iron warden's seal and put it in Muthu's hand in the hall. Corporal Kandan was the first to salute Devan as he walked out, and the garrison followed fist by fist.
The queen's night-guard have their wrist resin ridges pared smooth by a palace surgeon, so a slipped cuff shows a single seam; their throats are hidden with lime-and-ochre paste.
Before leaving Kettamala, Janu kissed both Devan and Neela on the forehead, the first time she had done so to Devan since he was twelve.
Neela counts the ache from a moon after the last night she turns; nobody has tested the count on purpose.
The pass-village watcher walks the ridge track, so Neela and Devan choose the wood road by the lower ford, half a day longer.
Ittan's tally book records four slash payments to the Resin House and a hook (delivery); a folded-wing sunbird is inked beside three lines and Neela cannot read it.
Neela takes the east stair and avoids the west stair without stating a reason.
Ittan asks only after his wife's willow-bark medicine and glances repeatedly at the dark corner of the guardroom; Neela judges he fears someone other than Devan.
Devan will not promise to let Neela choose in a life-or-death moment: 'I won't promise what I can't swear I'd keep.'

Eravi smears the escort's bark salve on Neela's nail with bare fingertip and his finger does not redden or burn, though resin burns non-odiyan skin; Neela notices and explains it away (cooked salve, horn-skinned hands). Plants Eravi (C-clue).
Neela tells Devan, 'Don't ask me what's in it', because Rema can put him under oath and he cannot lie; he agrees not to ask for three days. She has not told him the salve smells of resin.

Neela's rationalisation: First Guard's single smooth seam and clean-looking throat are not an odiyan's layered ridges, and the crown hangs unvouched odiyans, so she concludes crown men hiding something else.
Kannan says his mother's dog behaved like the hounds when a snake was in the thatch; Bhaskaran says the hounds are only wet.
Three of Neela's nails are split to the quick tonight; Eravi dresses them.
Devan has one 'I won't answer' pass each left from the question game; Neela spends hers on 'what are you'.

A rider from Kettamala brings Bhaskaran a strip in Rema's hand at the Resin House gate: she expects the Keeper's quire within two days or she comes for it. Devan tells Bhaskaran to say he is sitting on it and hearing all of it first, and risks a charge by doing so.
Asha at ten drew the west-stair parrot newel whole, saying a broken beak insulted the bird, and drew it mended on every note thereafter (consistent with F111).
Devan orders both ends of the master's-room passage left open with no man posted, moves the mat to the wall away from the door, and sets a brass water pot spout-left by it.
Pavi's green salve smells of crushed leaf and smoke, distinct from Eravi's tamarind-scented salve (F462).
Devan's palms are rope-burned from the well shaft rope and the pry bar.

Chathu's hunters shut the Resin House gate the day after Devan's party left, while the sun was high, on their own scouting of who remained. Vasu, sent by Pavi, saw it barred from the cairn before the tapping bell, was held overnight at the flooded ford, and reached Kettamala at first grey. Tonight's jar only confirms what Chathu already did.
Eravi's drunken wrong dose, the tapper's widow, and Fourth Guard's salve pot as a message conduit are established by this chapter.
Bhaskaran rode back with Devan the morning before the chapter; Vasu leads the six men and Pavi outside the Resin House wall in the sheds.
Eravi overheard the cart order in the passage outside the sickroom after the bear; he saw the sword hilt toward Neela during Devan's arrow fever.
Rema has been a clerk for thirty years.
Rema carried the second case five days from Kodiyur.
The queen's writ names Captain Muthu by office as holder of the pass seal in trust.
Rema offers to record Neela's departure by sunset as proof the warden harboured no unvouched odiyan.
Devan offers Rema the green-sealed last quire in the south range; Rema refuses to break the queen's seal or carry it to a high court that may not sit, and hands it back. Devan keeps it in his pack.

A faint folded-wing sunbird is pressed into the green thread of the sealed last quire where it crosses the wax, on both edges; the queen's own seal shows spread wings. Devan and Neela see it at dawn in ch 31. Breaking the queen's wax is treason in law.
The pass-village watcher found every Resin House scent-post gone cold at once and forty horses' dung on the goat path; Vellan met Kesu's grandson coming down it.
Neela read 'Sell to the crown when spent' on Vellan's leaf and took it as Chathu's threat to one man, not a trade; the 'Sold to the crown' sheet confirms the scale and pattern.
The thirty pages went to Kodiyur in a green-sealed box, and the sales ran over twenty years with rising sums.
Pepper hunters cut wild vine from the gullies in the dry months and use the shelter.
Kamalakshi laughs for the first time at the shelter.
Fourth Guard of Rema's escort is a young man, the youngest of the four; Second is also a man.
In the Resin House kennel aisle, the empty cage kept for Neela is the fourth from the end and Kirri's (tag nine) is the third from the end.
Devan sparred Muthu in the dawn pit on the seventh day (book 2, ch 9), his first round with Muthu in eight years; Muthu later says Devan still owes him the next seventh-day round.
Pepper the goat ate the last of the wedding marigolds off Kannan's garland.
Asha used to write Devan's letters for him.
There are eighty-six court stones between the well post and the kitchen door at Kettamala (Devan's count).
Thilak burned his own page and its intake roll in the gate fire-basket at the Resin House, choosing to lose his village and seller's record.
At the daylight reading Devan turned his back on Vellan and told him 'Go'; Vellan walked out of the Resin House into the wood, and Devan counted forty-one steps after the word.
On the last night at Kettamala Neela bit Devan's shoulder hard enough to break the skin; a matching welt rose on her own shoulder.
The forty's climb from Kettamala to the pepper hunters' shelter by the goat path took two days; on the first afternoon Kuttu's borrowed bay slipped on the ropes and Devan and Thilak held him.
Calling forced-turned members by their names, rather than their numbers, made some break off the hunt in the wood before dawn.

Neela has no memory of learning the fisherman's double hitch; Ammu always said a net-mender behind the sheds taught them both, but the knot has simply always been in Neela's fingers (hint of Nellimala childhood).
Meenu, Madhavi, Pavi, Thulasi, Kuttu, Kamalakshi and Thilak are among the forty-one odiyans at the shelter; Vellan sits by the door carving a bird.
The Company is a half-joking name Kuttu coined for the forty and the plank; it has not been formally agreed. Forty-one odiyans, Vellan included, share the thin resin.
From the shelter's ridge, after the cloud lifts, the sea and the Nellimala strand are visible; Neela recognises the bay's curve though she has never seen it from this side.
Devan counts fifty-eight Thurai ships plus two fishing boats, about sixty; he says a controlled raid is six to twelve boats.

Muthu is reading the crown's order from the gate chamber stair: the crown holds Kodiyur and the forts, the garrison stays inside the walls, and hill villages bear what comes. Kettamala's garrison will not go down.
Four members did not raise a hand in the resin vote and Neela directs the cup to them; the Company votes an even pinch for seven nights.
Pazhayangadi (Thulasi's home village) has been burned by the Thurai landing; Kalladi is holding with about a hundred raiders on the road.
Devan estimates the raiders will reach the Monkey Pass gorge, forty paces wide, in three days.
Muthu reads the crown's order from the gate chamber stair: the crown holds Kodiyur and the forts, the garrison stays inside the walls, and the hill villages bear what comes.

Devan puts his leave to go down and hold the gorge to the Company's vote and binds himself to it ('If the hands say no, I sit by this fire and hate it'). Vellan and Thilak volunteer after the vote is carried.
The resin vote: forty-two odiyans (the forty, Neela and Vellan); twenty-seven hands for an even split, eleven for the other plan, four abstain. The four abstainers get their pinch first.
Kesu's grandson's mother waits at the foot of the goat path with the goats; Kesu stays to hold the well.
First Guard is a few years past thirty, wears a green sash at the left hip, climbs alone with open hands and sleeves pulled to the knuckles. Her left wrist shows a single pared-flat seam.

Usha knows from the queen's household that a ledger page burned of itself at the Resin House on the new-moon night (Neela's self-naming), and asks what the naming cost; she does not name the shape. Neela tells her publicly only the wound-share.
Devan carries the oilcloth bundle (hide contract chit and the queen's payment writ, tied with red thread) in his pack on the hill, not in the shutter frame at Kettamala.
Usha says the pass-village watcher's scent log goes to a cell at Kettamala and on to whoever opens the prisoner's post, which is the queen's household. This matches F666 and F713.
Devan orders 'Nobody smears tonight' so no stranger can witness a turning; the Company obeys without asking why.
Usha is First Guard's given name, offered unasked; the letter calls the forty 'those who came down from the Resin House'.
Devan's 'Tuesday' nick while shaving: Neela finds the welt on her chin over her rice. Neela mentions it to Usha as a joke.

Usha knows from the queen's household that a ledger page burned of itself at the Resin House two nights past the new moon (the dusk of Neela's self-naming, not the new-moon night itself), and asks what the naming cost; she does not name the shape. Neela tells her publicly only the wound-share. Revises the earlier new-moon wording.
Neela tells Usha that Devan nicked his chin shaving 'three days back' and she found the welt over her rice. No weekday names are used.

At the end of ch 2 Neela and Devan state the cost of Usha's door aloud: Kodiyur is four hard days away and the raiders reach the gorge in three, so taking the door means Devan leaving the pass he swore to the Company's fire to hold, or Neela going alone.
After the assize Rema sent Chathu south to Kodiyur in a closed cart with her roll, to be held for the high court; he is now in the queen's cells under the palace rock.
Neela has never seen the palace at Kodiyur except as a shape from the quay; she knows only the fish-market lanes and the Chirayil north warehouse.

The Company's vote was 20 to hold the narrows with none going south, 22 for a party going south, with Thulasi abstaining; the resin was split even by hands, 37 to 6, with the six carrying their pinches in a leaf.
The six for Kodiyur are Neela, Pavi, Thilak, Madhavi, Kuttu and Meenu.

Neela recalls Rema ordering Chathu south to Kodiyur in a closed cart with her roll for the high court (F752). From Usha's remark that a Kettamala cell's post ends in the queen's household (F745), she infers he is now in the queen's cells under the palace rock, and admits she cannot be sure.
Corrects F754: the resin was split by hands as 36 pinches for the gorge and 6 for the road, 42 odiyans in all; Devan takes none.
Meenu was once held in a cage the width of a hunter's arm.
Ammu told Neela the page rule (a page held by its own subject cannot be read against her by anyone else) in the straw of the kennel.
Devan has grey in his hair.
After her page was read, Kamalakshi stood in the sun a long time and then ate two bowls of rice; her first laugh is still at the shelter (F717).
Chellam is a toddy-tapper's wife from Kalladi with a baby, camped by the Kettamala well; Gouri is another refugee whose mother is still on the road.
Bhaskaran's men lay a resin-pine beacon stack each dry season on the shoulder below the lightning boulder, watched by a pass-village boy.
The descent from the shelter to Kettamala takes two days with one cold night under the thorn and no resin smeared; the advance guard reaches the gorge a day or more earlier than Devan estimated.
Muthu houses the Company in the lower court as 'drovers' and the warden's guests for one night, as a loophole in the order to harbour no rogues.
Janu's right hand is wrapped in a cloth for a day-old burn, and she hands Neela things by the rim so their hands never touch; her eyes drop once to Neela's wedding bangle.
Parukutty has a cough (seen in the court at Kettamala).
The six for Kodiyur were to leave Kettamala by first light on the sea road; the gorge fight delays them.
Chellam's man tapped toddy on the Kalladi road before the raiders came up the coast.
Muthu now sleeps in the warden's chamber, at the end of the north range up its own stair; the stair door is visible from the guest room doorway, with lamplight under it.

Koman is the old guild watcher from the pass village above the gorge. He walked the hill edge for the Resin House eleven years, has not been paid since the House fell, and is hired by Devan's personal word at seven panam to the moon from Devan's own pocket.

The raiders' bronze signal mirror carries a small folded-wing sunbird scratched beside its handle on the back. Devan notices and does not understand it. Planted as clue C10, echoing the folded-wing sunbird in Ittan's tally book and the ledger stubs.

The Thurai advance guard is twenty-three men. The captured sergeant says they carry cutting-saws, mortar lime and seed barley, with orders to leave the vines and cooperative villages standing, and that the admiral expects the queen not to come.
Devan has a shallow knife slash on the outside of his right forearm from the picket fight. A matching welt rose on Neela's right forearm. She binds it with a strip torn from her cloth hem.
Corporal Kandan's nine volunteers include Vasu, Sankaran and Kuttan. Five others are unnamed on the page.
Corporal Kandan and nine volunteers (Vasu, Sankaran, Kuttan and six others) defy Muthu's order and come down from the wall to hold the cart road at the lightning boulder.

Devan sends the leopard (Neela) up the lip alone to look before Koman speaks; after Koman locates the mirror man, the rest of the Company goes up on Devan's word, 'Left of the cut. Alive, if you can.'

Koman, the old guild watcher from the village above the gorge, is hired on Devan's personal word at seven panam to the moon, paid from Devan's pocket. He reads twenty-three raiders and one man with brass on the lip.
The raiders' bronze signal mirror has a folded-wing sunbird scratched beside the handle (clue C10). Devan does not understand it.
At first light a glint flickers on the lip and Devan's count of six hundred runs out before the mirror is taken; it flashes only briefly and no answer is known.

The captured sergeant says the advance guard carries cutting-saws, mortar lime and seed barley, with orders to hold the pepper hills through the dry season and leave vines and cooperative villages standing, and that the admiral expects the queen not to come.
Vellan will not yet say Asha's last words: 'When I've earned saying it.'
Neela returns Kandan's gourd and says his name aloud; he answers 'Neela'.

Nellimala's stone footings lie on a slope near the shore under lantana; the Thurai camp there has 63 tents, three horse lines (22, 26, 24 animals), about 40-50 barley sacks, three sentries at the track end, and a half-built siege tower of ship timber on a cart bed, three men high.
Neela keeps a day-cloth cache in a dry crack under the lightning boulder, and Devan brings it warm inside his coat with rice and curd at grey.

A Thurai raider sleeping by the tower has fresh salt-and-clove-bark resin on his skin and old pale ridged scars on the inside of both wrists, a long jaw and a ring on his left thumb. Neela does not know what it means (clue C12).

Since Neela's self-naming no one can cage her without her own voice, so Devan's cheek-pebble is now a chosen ritual rather than a safeguard. The ration she smears came from the three noon trees Thilak tapped before leaving the shelter.
An old woman refugee mends a net with a bone needle in a pass village on the cart road and stares at Neela's hands as Neela unconsciously ties the double hitch in her sash.
Ponni is an old fishwife of Nellimala, now sleeping in Kesu's cattle shed in the pass village; she ran with baby Indu in her arm for the first bend of the goat path before Ammini took her.
Neela's mother Ammini was a net-mender of Nellimala who tied the fisherman's double hitch and went up the goat path after her daughter and did not come down.

At the second harvest two Thurai boats crossed the bar at slack water without a pilot, 'as if expected'. Men in grey waited at the top of the goat path with a flat cart whose tailboard bore a small, new yellow bird; one of them counted the youngest children as they were lifted onto it.
Neela remembers, at twelve or thirteen, seeing Chathu rewrite Kirri's rat-eaten page in resin-ink in his room, saying 'A master who saw you turn can always write you again.'
Devan tells Neela the grey-cloaked household man who recruited Muthu comes to mind, but notes the Kettamala garrison and many hill villagers also wear grey, and says he will not build on it.
The Company's members read their own intake rolls by the fire at the lightning boulder the night before the Kodiyur party leaves at first light.

Devan's count at the shelf: about fourteen hundred Thurai (sixty hulls, twenty-odd each) against forty-two odiyans, six of whom leave for Kodiyur next light, so thirty-six remain, plus forty garrison volunteers: seventy-six defenders. This replaces the outline's 'seventy odiyans', which conflicts with F740 (forty-two odiyans).
The Kodiyur party reached the shelf on foot with a pack pony at first light, and Neela stopped there to see Devan's wall plan; the scout attack delays their departure.

Bhaskaran's horn code for the queen's riders at the gate is two long notes, a short, and a long (distinct from F455's one long and two short for unarmed strangers). The horn carries down the cut from Kettamala to the lower narrows.

Devan takes a shallow arrow graze along his left upper arm, shoulder to elbow; a matching welt rises on Neela's left forearm. The outline's 'since the snow' is rendered as 'since the night at the Resin House', as there is no snow in Varanad's rules.
Devan kills a Thurai scout with a spear thrust before the man's blade rises, striking first for the first time in eight years. Four scouts die and two flee up the slope with Kandan's men in pursuit.
The dead scout's purse holds eleven new Varanad silver coins, all with the doubled lowest pepper leaf, matching Parukutty's coin and weighing the same to a grain.

Biju, a young garrison volunteer in a red headcloth, is posted as lookout on the lip above the shelf with a horn; the scouts climb the back of the cut and kill him silently. He is dead and stays dead, making Devan's count seventy-five.
Devan keeps his spear within arm's reach by habit since Raman died.
Defender count: seventy-six (thirty-six odiyans plus forty volunteers) against about fourteen hundred is eighteen apiece; Kandan adds 'nineteen once we've buried the first of us'.
Kandan's volunteers number forty here (outline); F776 gave nine, so the rest joined after.
Bhaskaran's horn for crown riders carries a mile down the cut from the Kettamala gate to the lower narrows.

The crown order case is tied with a green silk ribbon, which Pepper the goat eats off the rider's saddle and then bites his hand. Muthu's reply is written open in plain ink and sealed with one bead of black wax pressed with the iron warden's disc; the grey stick is left untouched.

Rema's escort wore pale green stiff cotton cuffs buttoned to the knuckle with two pegs and turned the wrist inward to take a cup; Muthu counted them during their four days in his gate chamber, and an escort member said drunkenly that a palace surgeon pares the guards' wrists each season.

The crown order is written in a clerk's round hand, the same hand as the household slip 'Say nothing, and your wife is kept' (F504). Muthu notices it while reading and says nothing; Neela does not yet connect it.
Biju, the volunteer killed at the shelf, was seventeen (Devan says so in the yard).

While reading the crown order, Muthu's thumb stops on one line; he reads it twice and glances at his belt pouch. Neela files it as the hard words (clue C11, matches the round clerk's hand of F808/F504).
Devan, before the yard, gives only the cost (a host three days off, Biju dead) and withholds the cut's place, depth and timing from the crown's rider; Neela notes the omission.
Neela carries a handful of lime thorns from the bush by the kitchen well, three each, for the noon signal; Devan pricks his thumb on the leopard tooth he wears on a cord at his chest.
Neela has six pinches of resin in a banana-leaf fold for the Kodiyur road and skips resin on the night before leaving; the last turning was five nights earlier at Nellimala.
The wound-share carries warmth and pleasure as well as hurt on the night they are together; a love bite leaves a matching mark on the other and they practise treating it as not a summons.
Devan hands Neela a warm cloth and a leaf packet of cold rice and curd at the departure.

The corridor lamp outside the guest-room door is a plain clay lamp on a hook by the stair, found lit and filled with sesame oil at the middle watch; the left forearm welt rises an hour down the hill road.
Neela moved the leopard tooth from her waistband to Devan's neck cord herself on the last night at Kettamala; he has worn it against his chest since (bridges F346 and F812).
Chami (a drover) and Rajan (a boy from Kalladi with a spear taller than himself) are the two other volunteers killed on the shelf, with Sankaran, on the first day.
Thurai ladders are lashed ship-timber with iron hooks, and the Thurai wear bronze caps; the assault is about three hundred men.
Kandan's men keep the names of the dead on a chalked roof tile, in imitation of Neela's barracks name tile.

Muthu writes his thirty-man sortie in the open post book in black wax and plain ink as 'to escort refugees from the pass villages', and takes the thirty from the garrison without the fort's full strength being counted.
Kesu's village is at the foot of the goat path, a half day below the shelf and behind the Thurai lines; the herald names it as the first to burn at dawn.
On the first noon Devan felt a sting on his left thumb mid-fight but could not count it; on the second noon he sees three clear welts and sits on a boulder until they fade.

The Kodiyur drying shed where off-duty night-guards meet is at the end of a lane behind the fish market, with three doors (front, side, and one behind the nets); the palace infirmary is said to have ears, so Thankam sees the guards there.
Neela's five companions (Thilak, Pavi, Madhavi, Kuttu, Meenu) entered by the Salt Gate behind a pepper cart and wait in a salt store near the tanneries; Neela went in alone by the Hill Gate.
Neela's disguise: green starched cotton cuffs pegged at the knuckle, and a throat paste of pass-village lime and potter's ochre that dries chalky; the wedding bangle sits under the left cuff.
Rukmini sells dried mackerel at the third stall from the weighing house, with scale-boy Pappu.
Sajan (Second Guard) is a man, bitter about the queen; Lata (Third Guard) is a woman loyal to the queen whose brother's wife received a death-gift reply; Sanu (Fourth Guard) is the youngest.
Sanu carried the notes for a year, given by a man in a grey cloak in the lower court who 'counted' him each time and never spoke; Sanu never read them.
Usha says the sea-stair landing guard change is at the sixth bell, takes sixty breaths, and leaves the landing empty for the last twelve (nine if it is blowing).
Chathu has been asking for Seventeen for three days, saying she would come.
Mani is the turnkey at the foot of the palace cell stair, who accepts Usha's word that Neela is a new guard carrying supper.
The cell stair has 104 steps; Chathu's cell is the eighth door, a rock cut three paces by four with a cot, bucket and sea slit.

The sea stair rises 110 steps from the water gate, roofed against spray, to a black wooden door in a screened passage; the queen's room is the third door beyond it. A red lacquer chest with a gold bird and a farm lock sits under its window and holds the crown leaf.
The queen sits audience in the long hall from the noon gun until the water-clock turns; the gun shakes the rock and covers a footstep.
Chathu's tin of sweets was still warm in a cell with no fire; Neela notes someone warmed it and does not ask who.
The queen sent her steward on the second day with a list of the forty names with blanks, asking Chathu to write the pages fresh; he has not answered.
Chathu is allowed only a pot of common ink and a reed; his fingertips are stained dry grey-brown, not tacky black resin-ink (clues C03/C17).
Chathu says he wept for Ammu in the cell the first night.
Usha promised two knocks if anyone came down the cell stair; none came before the grey-cloaked steward arrived.
Chathu was brought up to the queen's room each evening for four nights to write at her table, by the sea stair under guard, then returned to the cells.
The sea stair's foot lies at the water gate past the end of the lower-cell passage, where the landing guards change.
Neela wears a guard's boots from Usha's locker.

The sally is voted in the black hour before first grey; the Company is human that night by rotation, so the fifteen smear then, turn, and fall back into the thorn at the village edge before first light. Kandan's ten follow on foot by the goat path.
The Company's vote is twenty hands to sixteen for the sally. Kamalakshi votes hold and then takes the shelf wall; Thulasi votes sally; Vellan volunteers.
Devan announces the sally as his order under the Company's vote and tells Kandan his name goes first on the chalked tile of the dead if it fails.
The Thurai vanguard horse lines (about seventy horses) stand at the mill ford below Kesu's village; torches come up the lower road behind them.
Ponni says she told Kesu the warden had a wife who ties knots; she asks Devan where Neela is.

A Thurai boarding hook (iron, three-pronged, on a rope) tears across Devan's right ribs near noon in the lower narrows. He closes it with nine stitches of waxed silk using Kandan's curved needle. The long ladder-hook cut across his back from the previous day is still pulling.
Before she left, Neela told Devan she would go where the city was loudest; Devan reasons that in Kodiyur this means the noon gun, and so fears she may be on a stair at noon. He cannot warn her.
Devan pricks his left thumb three times with the leopard tooth from his neck cord, about an hour after noon, to signal late that he lives.
All fifteen odiyans of the sally came back up the cut at grey, shaking with the morning hunger; Thulasi took a horse's hoof on a foreleg and will limp for a month.
Rescued from Kesu's village: Kesu, Ponni and thirty more, thirty-two in all, as Devan counts.

Replaces F852: the fifteen odiyans of the sally turned back human at first light in the thorn below the village (F844), bare and shaking with the morning hunger, and climbed the back of the cut in blankets the villagers left, reaching the shelf at mid-morning. Thulasi took a horse's hoof on a foreleg (cracked, not broken through); she can walk but cannot hold a spear human this week, and Vellan stays by her. With the fifteen spent until dusk, tomorrow's shelf wall is sixteen hands thinner. No one died.
Rukmini lent a mackerel skiff for a day for four panam, no questions asked; Pavi sculls it under the cliff.

A stone-framed spray slot in the sea stair roof, a body wide, opens above Usha's landing; Neela enters by rope through it and leaves by the stair, past the landing and out through a fish wicket where porters bring in the palace catch.
Neela pricks her left thumb with three lime thorns half an hour before the gun, so Devan gets an early signal; his own late signal arrives an hour after noon as three welts.

The thirty crown-leaf pages are stiff pale leaves in black resin-ink, each with its intake roll looped on by green thread, resting on blue cloth in the chest; a folded-wing bird in thin brown line sits in each margin. The farm lock hangs open on the hasp.

The queen's petition answers are signed 'Nirmala' in full in a quick slanting hand, with no stamp or clerk copy; she pays one widow from her own purse. Neela hears the queen's warm voice say 'leave the shutters, I like to hear it'.
Cheru's widow of Kalladi is the topmost petitioner.
Of the thirty night-guards, twenty-two (Usha, Sanu and Sajan among them) agree to come at dawn; eight refuse, including Lata, who will take her page only from the queen's hand.
The hook welt at noon tears across Neela's right ribs under the arm, matching Devan's boarding-hook wound in ch 14.
Sanu's birth name is Chandrika, a tailor's daughter of Pallikara by the river, sold at seven; Usha's birth name is Ushakumari, a potter's daughter from a hill village.
At the shelter, Kamalakshi asked Neela what stops a master writing a page again; Neela answered that Chathu never needed to.
Usha's fresh crown-leaf page is dated and written the night before in the queen's hand with Usha as ledger number Four, and the queen leaves it and Chathu's forty fresh pages with Neela.
The queen says a rider leaves the Salt Gate at dusk carrying the same offer (three hundred spears and Kettamala restored) to Devan, so he will have it before Neela does.
The queen says she has known of self-naming for nine days, since Usha told her what a burning ledger page means.
Corrects F863: Sanu (Fourth Guard) is male; his birth name Chandrika, given after his mother's mother, is on his intake roll as a tailor's son of Pallikara, sold at seven.
Corrects F865: Usha's crown-leaf ledger number is Nineteen, not Four (Four is Thilak's, F632).

Neela half-notices that Chathu's grey-brown common-ink fingertips (F838) and his unanswered steward's list (F837) do not fit the forty black-ink pages the queen says he wrote at her table. She fails to resolve it under the queen's calm (clue C03/C17 stays live).
A brown, quick river runs below the lower narrows past a shingle bank where the cut meets the cart road; the near (Varanad) bank has thorn below the shelf.
Muthu brought eleven sheaves of arrows (forty to a sheaf) down the cut by handcart at midmorning.

The queen's letter to Devan is in a clerk's round hand with a few closing lines in her own slanting hand ('You will think it a lever. It is.'); it states that the same offer is put to Neela in Kodiyur.
Devan seals his reply with a bead of plain black wax and the print of his left thumb, because Muthu holds the iron disc; Muthu signs as witness.
A flat Thurai supply cart behind the siege tower carries a small, fresh yellow bird painted on its tailboard (echo of F791).
Koman reads scent and says the creature that swam the river is not any shape the Resin House ever made; he calls Devan 'warden' and Devan lets him.
Members of the Company have begun asking each other whom they would self-name to; Kuttu asked Vellan, who refused.
Devan and Neela's term, made in the tack room during the rain: 'say it before you do it'. In ch 17 Devan breaks it by answering the queen's letter before Neela can be told.
Devan addresses Rema as 'Justice Rema' in his letter, following the outline; F707 calls her a clerk of thirty years, so the title is an honorific his letter uses.
Kuttu (not Kamalakshi) asked Vellan whom he would self-name to; Vellan refused ('I've handed enough people my wounds'). Matches F877.
Muthu, now holding the iron disc, says he would hand it back tonight if a yes cost him it, yet urges Devan to accept the queen's offer for the pass.

Sajan (Second Guard) and Sanu (Fourth Guard) are brothers from Pallikara, sold two years apart to different houses; Sajan's intake roll names a younger brother sold at seven. Neither knew until Neela read the rolls. Sanu wants to self-name to Sajan; Sajan says he would bleed for him and would rather not.
Lata (Third Guard) refused her page in ch 16 but rode north anyway, joining at the Salt Gate at dusk, so the riders number twenty-two with her (one of the twenty-two who agreed stayed behind).
Neela took Chathu's tin of sweets from his cell and ate one there; she has not eaten another.
The ride from Kodiyur to the shoulder above the pass takes four days; the Company's 'nobody smears' order holds on the road, so no one turns.
Neela reinterprets the jackal call 'tomorrow, I will find you' as 'wait, I will be found', not a goodbye.
The queen gave Usha a folded strip of paper sealed in green wax, reading 'Ride with her. Press nothing.' Usha shows it unopened at the third post to get fresh horses.

Neela infers that the 'net-mender behind the sheds' Ammu credited was not real; the double hitch came from Neela's mother Ammini through Neela's own fingers, and Neela may have taught it to Ammu as a child.
Neela reads Ammu's jackal call as 'don't decide without me', given on nights Neela went off alone to settle something not hers alone.

Replaces F887: the queen gives Usha a folded strip sealed in green wax with the sunbird at the Hill Gate and speaks its line aloud in Neela's hearing ('Ride with her. Press nothing.'). Usha never breaks the seal; she shows it whole at the third post to get fresh horses.

Retires F886 ('wait, I will be found'). Neela reads Ammu's jackal call 'tomorrow, I will find you' as 'don't decide without me', given on nights Neela went off alone to settle something not hers alone. Her last hearing of it was in the Resin House yard before Ammu drew Vellan off (F252), with Neela in shape.

Neela remembers Devan putting a river pebble in his cheek before the Company's count on the gorge vote and saying a flat, careful 'yes' to the result that sent her south; this grounds her fear of his voice in the coming vote.
At the night camp the question-for-a-question custom of the Resin House long table is used round the fire; Kuttu proposes it and Madhavi remembers it.

Neela tips her six-pinch banana-leaf fold into the Company's noon-tree pot at the shelf and takes one even pinch like everyone else; the queen's riders take theirs from a green-waxed flat tin of crown resin Usha carried from the palace.
Neela missed the noon signal because the queen kept her in the sea room, standing at her elbow, for the whole hour on the day after the gun.
Two Company/garrison dead in the tower assault (Chami's cousin and a woman of Kalladi); seven hurt; all twenty-two queen's riders survive, three limping.
Usha has word that a crown column is a day and a half behind her riders on the road.
The Company's council summons is a great ram's horn kept at the cairn fire, one long bellow, distinct from Bhaskaran's gate code.

Before Neela turns on the shelf, Devan orders the wall pairs to face the road with backs to the shelf and count sixty, so the garrison does not witness any turning; Kandan turns round only after the animals are in shape.
Usha's word of the crown column comes from a rider of hers who came in off the road at grey.

Revises F900: Usha's word of the crown column reaches the council through Koman, the pass-village watcher, who read the road from the lip at grey; Usha confirms the banners are the queen's own. No extra rider of Usha's exists. Devan says he lost count of the dawns after nine.
The Company climbs the cart road to Kettamala's lower court for the council on Muthu's open leave; the cairn fire and shelf lie about a mile down the cut.

Pavi asks Thilak and he says yes; Kuttu asks Bhaskaran, who says yes at the gate arch and says he must tell his wife. Kamalakshi refuses everyone and Vellan refuses. Sajan neither accepts nor refuses Sanu.
Devan's written reply to the queen refused Kettamala and said the spears were not his to take or leave, and that the Company would answer for itself. Muthu witnessed it and the rider left by morning.
Koman reports the long shape in the river at the shingle bank from first grey through the tower fire. It took nothing and watched the shelf.
Usha confirms the queen rides with the column because the outriders go in pairs on both flanks when she is present; she read them from the lip with Koman at midday.

Repair terms after the breach in ch 20: tonight Neela will speak against Devan before the Company if she thinks him wrong, and at the gate tomorrow he will not answer for her. Devan tells her beforehand what he will say to the queen (he refused Kettamala alone; the Company has not voted; he will say nothing of what she is unless she does), and will stand a step behind her.
Corrects F905: Koman reports the long shape came into the river after the tower fell at the middle watch and watched the shelf until the stump stopped smoking. It took nothing.
The Company's council ended by agreeing that nobody answers the queen until she has spoken in the open at the gate; no vote on her offer was taken.
Devan took the oilcloth bundle (chit, payment writ, cut gift seal) from his pack and returned it to the shutter-frame hollow behind the third slat for the night.
The grey river pebble Devan left on the warden's chamber sill in book 1 is still there, undisturbed.
Devan tells Neela he will tell the queen to her face first, then read the payment writ aloud at the gate in daylight before the Company and the garrison.

Devan's chest/back at ch21: nine fresh silk stitches on the right ribs beside the old ford seam, and the ladder-hook cut across the back, dressed; Neela feels the right-rib ache while kissing past the stitches.
