At dawn Devan tells Neela the exact cost of reading the writ: three hundred spears under captains who do not know him, about seventy-odd defenders, fourteen hundred Thurai beyond the cut; he says the reading may cost the spears and the pass. The cut gift seal is in the bundle (Devan kept it in his sleeve, F071).

Defender count at ch21 dawn, per Devan: forty-two odiyans, twenty-two queen's riders and forty garrison volunteers (104), less six dead (Biju, Sankaran, Chami, Rajan and two more) = ninety-eight. Replaces 'seventy-odd' in F914.
Devan says he added the cut gift seal to the oilcloth bundle on the hill, alongside the chit and writ (refines F744).
Term set at dawn ch21: Devan reads the writ at the gate as his own account; Neela gives the Company's refusal and reasons in her own voice; Devan stands a step behind and does not speak for her.

At the gate, in one sentence, Devan told the queen that he holds a paper with her wax on it and will read it when Neela has answered, not before; the queen allows it and sets the answer at the dusk before the assault.
The queen met Asha once at a fair, where Asha argued with her about the price of pepper sacks.
Neela brought Chathu's sheaf of forty pages to the hall table so the queen's thirty and Chathu's forty lay side by side; the queen's smell bitter and scorched, Chathu's smell of lamp-black.
Parukutty's petition asks that the four widows' death-gifts be paid now, and that her son Chandu carry rice, not arrows; the queen pays from her own purse with a signed paper.
The queen's spies place the main assault two nights from the evening of ch22.
The queen met Asha once at the Kolathur fair, where Asha argued with her over the price of pepper-sacks and was right.
Lata (Third Guard), who refused her page, rode north with Usha's riders and is already on the shelf while the queen's column arrives; the other seven who refused ride with the queen.
The queen knows the eleventh step of the west stair from Rema's roll, which took down the physician Eravi's account of the postern and the eleventh step; she does not use any key.
After the Company's council, Kuttu hung the great ram's horn (F898) on the well post in Kettamala's lower court; Neela takes it down and sounds it to summon the Company.
The queen knows Devan carries the payment writ because her people watch him; she names it as the bundle he carries up and down her hills.
Neela tells the Company she will answer the queen at dusk the day after tomorrow, and will tell them her intended words that night at the cairn fire first.
Captain Haran is the queen's captain of the crown spears: broad, grey-moustached, about fifty. His second is Sethu.
The council vote on Devan's line plan carries five to one; Captain Haran votes no but agrees to hold the centre 'under the table', not under Devan.
Vellan will hold the narrowest place at the top of the cut alone, unbound, so no one bleeds for him; he nearly gives Asha's last words and defers them to 'after'.
Kamalakshi carves a bad wooden bird with Vellan's knife and gives it to him; he keeps it inside his shirt.
Kamalakshi is described as perhaps nineteen, thin, with cropped hair.
Neela told the Company her intended answer at the cairn fire the night before (as promised in ch 22); the answer to the queen was moved from the dusk to the afternoon of ch 24 after Koman's report.
The queen keeps the unread oilcloth writ question open: Devan does not read it, and the queen says she knows what it says and would rather it were read after the ladders come down.
Sanu chooses Kandan to self-name to; Sajan stays among the four unready guards with Lata and two others. Thulasi names to Madhavi. A crown spear-captain with a grey moustache is chosen by a guard.
Bhaskaran's wife and Kuttu's choice of him were arranged at the cairn fire an hour before dusk; Bhaskaran applies the resin to Kuttu's throat because Kuttu is shaking.
Queen Nirmala now feels the share with Usha and admits 'it does sting'.
Kandan asked Sanu's name once on the cart road when Sanu's horse went lame at the boulder, and has used it since.

Company namings burn witness entries from Chathu's forty fresh leaves held on Neela's knee; crown leaves burn only in the queen's case when a guard names. Intake rolls stay whole. Four crown leaves remain for the four unready guards.

The heavy-set queen's guard who said no in Kodiyur and yes at dusk is paired with Vasu, a Kettamala spearman (his mother keeps ducks at Kalladi). Her shape is low, quick and grey-brown, unnamed. She is cut across the shoulder; Vasu drops under the share and the line gaps.
The spear goes through under Devan's right collarbone and out at the back; his right hand is dead and will not close. The shaft is broken off short by an unseen hand.
Neela takes scored welts on the ribs and shoulder in leopard shape, and Devan feels hook drags along his side, before the spear.
Vellan leaves his unbound post at the narrow place at the top of the cut to fill the gap; the narrow place is open behind the line when Devan loses consciousness.

The faltering pair at the bend of the line is a slight guard from Usha's riders, unnamed, paired with Vasu, a Kettamala spearman (his mother keeps ducks at Kalladi), at dusk; ch24 did not show this pairing. Her shape is low, quick and dark and goes unnamed. She is cut across the shoulder; Vasu drops under the share and the line gaps. Replaces F941.

The spear goes through under Devan's right collarbone and out at the back; his right hand is dead and will not close, so the two-finger marma strike he used on a raider captain before the garrison, his first since the lower ford, was his last. The shaft is broken off short by an unseen hand.
Neela takes scored welts on the ribs and shoulder in leopard shape, and Devan feels hook drags along his side, before the spear.
Vellan leaves his unbound post at the narrow place at the top of the cut to fill the gap; the narrow place is open behind the line when Devan loses consciousness.
Thankam is the queen's surgeon: a broad woman past fifty with grey hair tied in a green strip, who closes Devan's wound with clamp, needle and waxed silk.
Thankam says the spear cut the nerve behind the collarbone; the shoulder and lung will mend, but the nerve to the right hand is cut and may take a year to regrow, if the hand ever closes hard again.
Queen Nirmala has a hand-long red welt on her left forearm from Usha's wound; she holds the lantern for Thankam, kneeling in blood.
The wounded are tended in a pocket against the rock at the rear of the shelf, on a cart tarpaulin under a hooded lantern hung from a stake.

At dawn Kandan and Muthu turn their backs as Neela turns back, and Muthu passes her a blanket; she rests two fingers on the healing point a hand's breadth under Devan's jaw at the hollow of the throat.
Neela opened her shuttered lamp once, a thumb's width, when Asha came down the west stair; Neela does not remember doing it. Vellan watched from the landing in bear shape.
Devan is carried up the cut on a guard-shed door with its strap hinge still on; Thankam binds his dead right arm to his chest with a green sash.
Vellan is opened by a hook from hip to ribs and dies unbound, so no wound-share. His dead hand holds Kamalakshi's bad bird.
The queen has burned twenty-six of the thirty crown-leaf pages at the namings; four remain, matching the four unready guards.
The Company is down to about thirty-odd of forty-two odiyans at dawn, with no individual deaths named other than Vellan.

Queen Nirmala states the roll's price: the first name written by daylight before every witness binds that person to the Company's vote and makes her the crown's first name to answer for whatever the Company does.

Vellan waited in bear shape low on the west stair, by the grate under the eleventh step, in the wall's shadow; Asha saw Neela's thumb of lamplight at the foot first and the bear only when nearly on it.
Devan is carried up the cut on a guard-shed door with its iron strap hinge; Muthu and Kandan carry him, and Thankam binds his dead right arm to his chest with a green sash.

At dawn Vellan sits in human form against the rock at the narrow place behind a half circle of Thurai dead, opened by a hook from hip to ribs, holding Kamalakshi's bad bird. A fifteen-year-old Thurai boy lies at his feet and Neela promises to see him buried.

Neela remembers opening her lookout lamp once, a thumb's width, only when Vellan says so. She says she counted to three hundred and ten at the stair foot after Asha died, and had never told anyone the number. Devan says he will carry half of it.
The Company is thirty-odd of forty-two at dawn, with no deaths named except Vellan.

The crown leaf is now in a flat green-lacquered leather case, scorched along one edge, brought up from the red lacquer chest (F834) in the night. Twenty-six leaves have burned of themselves at the namings and four remain.
Queen Nirmala states the roll's price: the first name written binds that person to the Company's vote and makes her the crown's first name to answer.

Eleven of the forty have not yet self-named and have no name beside their fresh pages. The queen claims Chathu's forty pages as the crown's because they were written at her table, and says Neela holds them 'on loan'.
Thilak supplies a clean crown leaf from the queen's green case and a cracked pot of plain clerk's ink and a chewed reed; the roll is laid on a board across two buckets by the well.
Usha writes her full birth name, Ushakumari, on the roll. Kandan signs with his village, Mathoor.
Janu lights a plain sesame-oil lamp on the bottom step of the west stair beside the parrot newel at noon, and says she will light it every noon she is in the house.
At dawn Neela told Janu what Vellan said about the shuttered lamp at the foot of the west stair; this is why Janu lights the lamp at noon.

Neela answers the queen's claim on the paper by offering her the roll itself, written on a crown leaf; the queen backs off ('Keep your roll. I want the pages.') but keeps her claim on the four guards' pages and the eleven unnamed pages of the forty.
Garrison men (Kandan, Bhaskaran) sign the roll, which reaches sixty names.
A Thurai herald asks the queen for a three-day truce at the stakes; Kandan counts about forty red-crested officers' caps among the dead, and the host withdrew to the beach under sergeants.

The queen never read any of Chathu's forty pages at night; she watched him write them over four evenings and did not wish to test a leaf on a stranger. Neela finds them dry-inked and without resin smell.

Chathu's tin of warm sweets and the note 'Written off. Paid in full. C.' in common grey-brown ink reach Neela by the palace post with the column's last rider, handed over by a steward of the queen's household.
Neela has checked every village on the thirty crown-leaf intake rolls against Devan's border roll of raids and finds each was raided in the year its child was taken.

CORRECTS F940 (flag for S7): at the ch24 namings the scorching witness entries were on each member's own handed-back Resin House page, which Neela held on her knee beside Chathu's sheaf. Chathu's forty leaves are plain ink and only curled in the heat; they never burned. Neela realises this in ch29.

Chathu's tins of sweets: eleven before her eleven killings, one in the kennels, one on the Resin House gatepost, and one carried out of his cell (the warm tin in ch29 arrives by palace post). Corrects any 'twelve before a killing' count.

Neela cites Sanu's Pallikara as a crown-leaf intake village burned this season (not Thulasi's Pazhayangadi, which belongs to the forty); every village on the thirty rolls was raided the year its child was taken.
The high court sat nine days before Rema reached Kettamala and entered Asha's murder and the pass sales as one conspiracy; it authorised Rema to record any charter made in daylight before witnesses.
Devan took the oilcloth bundle from the shutter-frame hollow at dawn of the day of the reading and carried it against his ribs.
The queen asks for one night and will answer at noon at the old watch-house on the shoulder above the narrows, which Neela requests for the Company's hall.
Lata self-names to Usha and Kamalakshi self-names to Janu at dusk, with the garrison facing the wall; shapes are not spoken on the page.

Devan asks Rema to enter his binding to Neela, odiyan, on the high court's roll, a crown record naming him as harbouring an odiyan in his own voice; Rema warns it goes to Kodiyur and Neela confirms it in public.

Usha takes a second wound-share with Lata, so she now bleeds for both Lata and the queen; Lata can be caged only with Usha's voice joined to her own, and the queen's old witness claim on Lata is voided.
Rema's four escort at the hall are bailiffs in borrowed green sashes; her original escort now stands with the Company.
Devan has hated the smell of resin for twelve years (since border school, F041).
Neela has a smudge of Thilak's ink on her wrist at dusk (no resin; she does not turn).
At dusk Neela, back turned, tells Devan by the sound of footsteps who steps forward, by name only, never shape.
The old watch-house on the shoulder above the narrows is chosen as the Company's hall.
Kamalakshi tells Janu she 'sat up with a lamp for the lot of us'.
Janu complains of the cairn-fire rice when she is bound to Kamalakshi.
Chathu is sentenced, at Neela's asking, to keep and tend the kennels at the groves for life under Pachan, gagged from dusk to dawn, no writing, no leaving.
The charter orders the 'Sold to the crown' sums repaid to the named members from the crown's treasury on the first day of the dry season.
The old watch-house has a rusted gate fire-basket; Muthu lends the Company his tent on the shoulder behind it.
Devan retains faint sensation in his dead right hand and feels Neela's welts and touch through the wound-share.

knowledge.knows: Her contract terms: kill Devan in his chamber so it looks like a leopard kill, before the pass closes.
Her only witnesses are Chathu and Ammu, and her page is in the ledger.
She was lookout on a hill-fort job six years ago where a young woman died. She was moved there blindfolded and does not know which fort.
She does not know the buyer of her contract, her birth name, or the self-naming loophole.
The witness rule, and that Asha's bear wounds inside the walls mean an odiyan contract killed her.
Forged pass-tokens with real council wax reach Thurai raiders. He does not know who sells them.
The council pressed the marriage, and he distrusts the bride.
The self-naming loophole, told to no one. She has had no answer to her letters to Kirri.
Every member's shape and page; that release is a lie; the buyer of Devan's contract and the queen's seal on it.
He killed Asha and Neela was lookout. He suspects release is a lie.
He bought Devan's contract, sells extra pass-tokens, and planned to take the pass-seal from Devan's widow.
Her secret treaty with Thurai, her seal on the contract writ, and the crown leaf of night-guard pages.
He reports on Devan to the queen's household. He knows nothing of the contract or the treaty.

timeline.event: Neela is born in a village on the coast side of the Monkey Pass.
Raiders burn Neela's village. At 6 she is sold to the Resin House.
Ammu, age 5, is brought to the Resin House.
Neela's first turning at 16, witnessed by Chathu and Ammu (14).
Devan, 24, kills a surrendering raider captain with a marma strike and stops sparring.
Asha, 22, is killed on Kettamala's west stair by Vellan. Neela, 21, keeps watch.
Devan, 27, is made warden of Kettamala.
Kirri is 'released' and secretly caged in the kennels.
Neela and Devan marry at sunset. That night Devan secretly witnesses her turning.
Monsoon closes the Monkey Pass. This is the contract deadline.
